### Interactions

- **Candidate keys and sharding.** `unique contentRef { site, body.digest }` reaches the shard root through `site`, satisfying tables.md:161-176 unchanged. The alternative — keying on the digest alone — would make every distinct payload its own shard root by tables.md:172, which is why dedup is scoped per root rather than globally. `body.digest` and `body.length` are key-eligible under the existing rule that a virtual column qualifies if it is immutable for the life of the row (tables.md:213-220); a `Blob` value is immutable by construction, so both qualify and `updated_at`'s exclusion does not apply.
- **The derived-key meaningful/degenerate rule.** A `Blob` column cannot be a group key or survive a projection as an identifying column, so a derived table over a blob source derives its key from the non-`Blob` columns only. Projecting `{ body.digest }` preserves a meaningful key; projecting `{ body }` does not, and therefore blocks incremental refresh, pins the source against `deprecate`, and makes the result read-only — all three consumers of the distinction firing correctly with no new rule.
- **The effect ladder.** The single sharpest restriction: octets are unreadable in `Pure`, `Read`, and `Tx`. A functor that must parse a payload runs in `Effect` off a queue. This is the same missing lift that keeps external calls out of a commit, applied to unbounded local reads — and it is what preserves functor transparency, because the optimizer can cost `body.length` and cannot cost `body`.
- **Append-only storage and the version chain.** The decisive interaction. A row version is a full row image (which is what makes the zero-copy read pointer arithmetic rather than a chain walk), so `Bytes` at 1 MB re-appends 1 MB on every write of any field. Chunks are separate component rows with their own locators, so a `Blob` pays only when the field itself is written. Content addressing then makes even that a one-time cost: a digest-keyed content row can only be inserted, so its version chain is length 1, and superseding it orphans the old row into the existing prune path rather than accumulating versions forever.
- **`Doc` shredding.** `Doc` and `Blob` do not overlap and do not compete. `Doc` is for tree-shaped data whose shape you want to discover; `Blob` is for octets you will never query into. They compose in one direction only: a `Doc` above `chunk_size` stores its authoritative bytes as a `Blob`, which removes `Doc`'s unstated frame ceiling while leaving HMAC verification and the shredded-tree-as-view rule untouched.
- **Access asserts on read.** One assert evaluation per request, on the owning row — chunks are not independently addressable, because nothing outside the parent's subtree may reference a component (traits.md:221). A public asset table declaring no `authed_user` assert pays nothing at all, which is what makes serving from a row competitive with a static file.
- **Functor transparency.** Preserved, and it is the reason for the `where`-over-`digest`-and-`length`-only rule. Admitting octets into a predicate would produce functor terms the optimizer cannot cost and static access analysis cannot bound, which is exactly the property OQ-001 says the GADT DSL exists to keep.
- **Replication traits.** `Blob` is rejected on `Reference` and `Configuration`, because both replicate to every server and a `Reference` insert *is* a schema commit. This is what breaks api-and-rendering.md:68's claim that a theme carries a stylesheet: the theme row keeps the manifest, the octets live in a data-classed table or are generated by the render functions that are already function-valued `Reference` columns.
- **Materialization.** Unchanged, and deliberately so. A `Blob` is not a materialized view and is not proposed by the maintenance queue; there is nothing to arrange for a byte range. The chunk chain is real storage with real graph entries, the same status `aggregates.md` gives rollup levels for the same reason — a materialized view is recomputable by definition, and a payload is not.
- **Relocation, compaction, and pruning.** All three carry unchanged. Relocation rewrites a `log_index` value and is free per chunk (storage.md:61-67). Compaction is lossless and now also reclaims the gap left by a scrubbed chunk chain. Pruning is unchanged: `retain` remains `LogData`-only, and a `UserData` blob leaves only by orphan-prune, `erase`, or `scrub`.
- **Erasure.** `erase` on a `Personal` table cascades to the blob through the FK chain for free (integrity.md:386-388), because the content row reaches the shard root the same way every other dependent does. No new eligibility rule.
- **Component ordinals.** The one place this design leans on something currently underspecified. `traits.md:199` and `transaction-graph.md:475-491` define the ordinal per parent, not per (parent, component table). A table with two `Blob` fields — or two `Doc indexed` fields, which is already possible today — needs chunk *n* of one not to collide with chunk *n* of the other. Flagged, not fixed.

### Alternatives rejected

- **Widen `Bytes` to unbounded.** Loses the distinction the whole design turns on. Every `Bytes` field becomes potentially unbounded, so `unique`, `==`, and key membership would have to be rejected on the 32-byte digests and wrapped keys that use `Bytes` today (auth.md:318,390; integrity.md:208). Two types, one bounded and one not, is the cheaper answer.
- **`Bytes chunked` as a storage clause, parallel to `Doc indexed`.** Tempting because the shape matches exactly, but it is a false parallel and it costs a reserved word. `indexed` requests a *derivable* view over bytes that remain authoritative in the row; `chunked` would move the authoritative bytes. And chunk size tracks hardware, so under traits.md:141-171 it is a `Configuration` row and does not belong in a declaration at all.
- **`Blob` as `:>` into a generated content table.** Genuinely more FK-shaped than `Doc` is, since the row holds a digest rather than the bytes. Rejected because it forces the author to name a generated, `internal`-visibility table in a user declaration, and because `Doc indexed` already settles that generating sibling tables does not change the token.
- **A generated engine-managed content table with automatic cluster-wide dedup.** Rejected three ways. A digest-only key makes every payload its own shard root (tables.md:172), so every read becomes a cross-shard join. There would be no FK edge for orphan detection, so pruning would need a refcount scan rather than the existing graph walk. And cross-tenant dedup is a confirmation oracle — "does anyone already have this exact file" becomes observable through storage accounting and upload timing. Author-declared dedup with `unique { root, body.digest }` gets all three right and adds no machinery.
- **Content-defined chunking (Rabin / FastCDC).** Buys sub-file dedup across near-identical payloads; costs O(1) byte-offset-to-ordinal, which is the hot read path. The premise is also weaker than it sounds: a rebuilt bundle is not a one-byte change, because minifiers, hashed module ids, and source maps perturb the whole file. Where per-deploy delta genuinely dominates, the correct answer is not to store the artifact at all.
- **An out-of-log side file, or an object-store pointer as a first-class type.** Breaks "the log is the graph", creates a second durability domain outside `verify shard`, and forces relocation, compaction, and scrub each to grow a second code path. A pointer to an external object is expressible today as a `Text` URL plus a `Bytes` digest and needs no type.
- **Chunks as a `Component` of the row *declaring the field*, with no separate content row.** This is what the design does — but with the author free to add a content row for dedup. Making the content row mandatory and engine-generated was rejected above; making it impossible was also rejected, because without an insert-only digest-keyed row there is no orphan-prune path and a blob table accumulates forever.
- **A `Blob` chunk linked list (`next :> Chunk`).** Rejected on a settled decision: railroad.md:958-961 declines to reserve `next` as a field name precisely because "a field named `next` would be a link in a hand-rolled linked list, which the transaction graph makes unnecessary". Component ordinals are the ordering.
- **Digest-joined chunks inserted before their parent, to allow multi-transaction assembly.** Would remove the one-transaction ceiling, and fails on anchoring: `assert` requires every source reached along a declared `:>` edge rooted at `self` (railroad.md:251-256), and a join on a digest value is not an edge. Left open as OQ-038 rather than forced.
- **A `Content` or `Asset` trait instead of a type.** A trait declares what a table *is*; a payload is a *value* in a field, and modelling it as a table shape would make every asset table hand-roll reassembly, digesting, length, and range reads. `Doc` is the precedent for a type whose storage is a generated component tree.
- **A `retain` chain on a `UserData` blob table.** Would give a declarative discard path, and it inverts a settled rule: `retain` is `LogData`-only because occurrences are prunable and entities are not (traits.md:107-111, aggregates.md). Orphan-prune over content-addressed rows gets the same effect without touching that boundary.
- **A byte-range operator in the query language.** Invites a substring operator over unbounded values, which the optimizer cannot cost and static analysis cannot bound. Ranging belongs in the transport, computed from `ordinal`, the way content negotiation does.

### OQ impact

- **OQ-005 (Schema DSL Syntax, ✓ ANSWERED)** — amend in place with one bullet. `Blob` is a new primitive for immutable, content-identified octets of unbounded length, stored as a generated `Component` chunk chain rather than in the row frame. **No production changed and no word was reserved** — type names are ordinary identifiers, and `body.digest` in a `UniqueDecl` was already grammatical. It carries two virtual columns, `digest` and `length`, key-eligible under the existing immutable-for-the-life-of-the-row rule, which is what makes dedup an ordinary `unique { root, body.digest }` rather than a mechanism. `unique`, `indexed`, `order by`, `group`, `==`, and key membership are rejected on the field itself and admitted on both virtual columns; a `where` may reference only those two, because the octets are unreadable in `Pure`/`Read`/`Tx` and a functor that must inspect them runs in `Effect` — the effect ladder applied to unbounded local reads rather than to external calls. Rejected on `Reference` and `Configuration`, since a `Reference` insert is a schema commit replicated to every server. `Hashed Blob` rejected (`digest` already is the one-way projection); `Encrypted Blob` admitted, reading `Sealed` and revealed only in `Effect`, so the zero-copy claim is untouched. `Bytes` is unchanged and stays correct below ~64 KiB. Names considered and rejected: `File` (there is no file), `Asset` (web-specific), `Content` (a likelier field name than type name), `Stream` (`Behavior` owns the time axis), and widening `Bytes` (would force rejecting `unique` and `==` on the digests that use it today). `chunked` was considered as a storage clause parallel to `indexed` and rejected: `indexed` requests a derivable view over bytes that stay authoritative, while chunking moves them, and chunk size tracks hardware so it is a `Configuration` row rather than syntax.
- **OQ-004 (Storage Engine, ✓ ANSWERED)** — amend in place with one bullet. Payloads never enter LMDB: `log_index`'s value is 12 bytes and `head_index`'s is 14, so the frequently-assumed LMDB value limit is not a constraint here. The ceiling is the log frame, which carries one whole `TxNode` including every mutation in the transaction. Cap'n Proto limits not previously recorded and now stated in `storage.md`: a `Data` field caps at 2^29-1 bytes (~512 MiB), a single segment at ~4 GiB of words, and the default reader traversal limit is 64 MiB. Chunks are `Component` rows, so the existing one-contiguous-range-scan property and `UserData`'s containment clustering carry the payload read path with no addition, and `ordinal` is the chunk index. The consequence that decides the threshold: a row version is a full row image, so an in-frame payload is re-appended on every write of any field of the row, while a chunk chain is not — which puts the `Bytes`-to-`Blob` crossover near 64 KiB rather than near any hard limit.
- **OQ-035 (Extent Size, Segment Period, and Shard-Group Formation)** — add two numbers to the open list, same species as the ones already there. `chunk_size`, which should divide the extent size so a chunk never straddles an extent boundary, with a starting range of 256 KiB to 1 MiB pending measurement. `max_blob_bytes`, the per-blob ceiling, starting range 64-256 MiB, bounded by what a primary should build in memory and ship to two secondaries before a commit returns. Both are `system.shards.BlobPolicy` rows with a per-server override, the `ExtentPolicy`/`ExtentOverride` shape, so a wrong default is tunable rather than fatal.
- **OQ-036 (Erasure, PII Scrubbing, and Shard Quarantine, ✓ ANSWERED)** — amend in place with one bullet. Scrubbing a chunked field writes one scrub node per chunk, each preserving its own chunk's length so no locator moves, and the disclosed total is `body.length`, which is already a queryable column — so unlike the scalar case the gap discloses nothing new. Verification reuses the existing definition verbatim: the octets verify if they hash to `digest`, or if divergence is covered by the `after` of a scrub node. `digest` is not re-derived after a scrub, because it is the row's identity and its constraint's key, and re-deriving it would rewrite history to conceal the act. Scrubbing a deduplicated payload destroys it for every referring row, bounded to one shard root because dedup is scoped there — which the diagnostic must name.
- **NEW: OQ-038 — Assembling a payload larger than one transaction.** GENUINELY OPEN, and a mechanism question rather than a number, which is why it is not folded into OQ-035. One blob write is one transaction and therefore one frame, so `max_blob_bytes` is a hard ceiling rather than a tuning knob. Assembling across transactions requires chunks to exist before their `Component` parent, which the trait forbids — a component is created with its parent and cannot be reparented. Every workaround checked breaks something settled: a chunk linked list reintroduces the `next` field OQ-005 declined to reserve; digest-joined chunks with no FK leave the completeness `assert` unanchored, which the anchoring rule forbids; an out-of-log side file breaks 'the log is the graph' and puts bytes outside `verify shard`; a staging table plus an `Effect` handler gets the bytes across many commits but still needs one final transaction carrying the whole payload. Options: (a) accept the ceiling and answer oversized objects with a manifest row plus an external store; (b) relax the `Component`-created-with-parent invariant for a generated chunk table only, which needs a story for a half-assembled parent that is visible; (c) admit a digest-joined chunk table and widen `assert` anchoring to cover a generated key join. Wants a decision before any upload path is built, and (a) is the current recommendation.

### Implementation notes

**Parser.** Nothing. `Blob` resolves through the ordinary type namespace and `body.digest` is an existing `FieldPath`. The work is in the resolver: recognize `Blob` in `FieldDecl` position, reject the six clauses, restrict the `where` scope to the two virtual columns, and reject the type on `Reference`/`Configuration` tables.

**GADT DSL.** One new term is needed and it is deliberately narrow — a `BlobHandle` carrying `digest` and `length`, with no elimination form in `Pure`/`Read`/`Tx`. The octet-yielding eliminator lives only at `Effect`, which is what makes "unreadable in a functor" structural rather than a check. This mirrors how `commit :: Tx a -> Effect a` carries the no-external-calls rule by a missing lift: here the missing thing is a `Blob -> Read Bytes`.

**Storage.** The largest piece. Chunking on write (fixed `chunk_size`, digest accumulated streaming so the payload is never fully resident), one `Component` row per chunk in the mutation list, `digest` and `length` written to the parent frame. Read is the existing component range scan with an ordinal bound. The frame builder needs a guard on `max_blob_bytes` and the Cap'n Proto reader's traversal limit has to be raised deliberately, with the raised value recorded — 64 MiB is the default and it will silently reject a 100 MB frame otherwise.

**Planner.** Two things. A projection naming a `Blob` yields a handle, never octets, so the plan carries a stream node rather than a value. And `body.digest` must be recognized as an indexable column so `where body.digest == d` is an index probe against the `unique` constraint rather than a scan — this falls out of the existing digest-partitioned unique index (`distribution.md:288-289`) and needs no new index type.

**Replication.** No protocol change: chunks are ordinary component rows in the delta. The only addition is the `DurabilityPolicy` lookup already keyed by table path.

**Scrub.** The existing per-frame zero-and-rechecksum, iterated over the chunk range, with one scrub node per chunk. Reuses the loop; does not need a new primitive.

**HTTP layer.** The real new surface. A serve mode that streams a chunk range with `ETag`/`Content-Length`/`Accept-Ranges`, `Range` and `If-None-Match` parsing, `304` short-circuit before any chunk read, and the `nosniff`/`Content-Disposition` policy. This should be a `FormatFunctor` row (`api.md:52-57`) rather than special-cased in the dispatcher, which keeps it inside the self-hosting story.

**CLI.** `--format raw` gains the single-`Blob` case; every other format renders the handle. Guard against a multi-row projection so `raw` cannot concatenate payloads.

**Spike worth doing before committing to numbers.** Extend `spikes/capnproto` with a chunked-payload case: confirm the `Data` cap and the traversal limit empirically, measure the chunked write path against a single large `Data` field at 1/10/100 MB, and measure a range read against a full read to confirm the containment-clustering claim holds for chunk chains as it does for shredded documents. That gives OQ-035 the measurement it asks for.

### References

- Git's object model — content-addressed immutable blobs plus a mutable ref, with unreferenced objects collected by reachability. The direct precedent for §3: content addressing is what turns an append-only store's unbounded growth into a reachability problem, and DataCode already has the reachability rule ('only orphaned branches are truly deletable').
- Subresource Integrity (W3C) — `<script integrity="sha384-…">`. Demonstrates that the digest is the interoperable artifact a browser actually wants from a deploy manifest, which is why the manifest recommendation in §7 is not a consolation prize.
- RFC 9110 §8.8.3 and §14 (HTTP Semantics) — strong versus weak validators, and Range/Content-Range. A digest over exact bytes is a *strong* validator, which is what licenses `If-Range` and byte-range resumption; a mtime-derived ETag would not be.
- Dropbox / Mega client-side deduplication attacks (Harnik, Pinkas & Shulman-Peleg, IEEE S&P 2010, 'Side Channels in Cloud Services: Deduplication in Cloud Storage') — cross-tenant dedup as a confirmation oracle. The security argument for scoping dedup to the shard root in §3.
- Amazon S3 multipart upload — the standard shape of the problem OQ-038 names: parts uploaded independently and a final 'complete' call that materializes the object. It works because S3's object is not a row in a graph with a parent-created-with-child invariant; naming the difference is what makes OQ-038 a real question rather than a copy.
- PostgreSQL TOAST — out-of-line storage of oversized attributes in a side table keyed by OID and chunk sequence, transparent to the query planner. Closest relational precedent for §2, and the shape DataCode gets for free because `Component` already supplies the chunk table, the ordering, and the free parent link.
- Cap'n Proto encoding specification — the 2^29-element list bound on `Data`, single-segment addressing, and the traversal-limit security setting. The source of the ceilings in §4 that `storage.md` currently does not record.
- Content-defined chunking: Muthitacharoen, Chen & Mazières, 'A Low-Bandwidth Network File System' (SOSP 2001), and Xia et al., 'FastCDC' (USENIX ATC 2016). What was rejected in §2 and what it would have bought — the papers are also the source of the caveat that CDC's gain depends on insertion-shaped edits, which minified bundles are not.

### Adversarial critique

**Fatal objections**

- **`retain` is NOT `LogData`-only. The docs have a section titled the opposite.** `aggregates.md:322` heads `### \`retain\` on \`UserData\` is admissible and rare`, and its first sentence is: "`retain` names a table, and nothing in it requires that table to carry `LogData`." `aggregates.md:298-299` reinforces it: "The rule is about the chain rather than about the trait, which is why it extends unchanged to `UserData`." Neither cited source supports the proposal: `railroad.md:417-420` is about `prune`, a different verb, and `traits.md:107-111` says `LogData` is prunable, not that `retain` is exclusive to it. The proposal asserts the false rule in four load-bearing places (pushback §1, §8's opening, `alternatives_rejected` #11, `oq_impact` OQ-036) and **rejects the correct answer because of it**. The existing zero-new-syntax discard path is the no-binding form at `aggregates.md:164-170`: `retain app.web.Content` / `for 90 day` / `, drop`. `aggregates.md:343` confirms `UserData` pruning is row-level; `aggregates.md:377-379` confirms a parent's `Component` subtree prunes with it, so the chunk chain goes automatically. This satisfies "discarding is never manual" (the chain is written) and "silence means keep" (no chain = never pruned).

- **There is no row-level `prune`, so "orphan-prune" is not a mechanism that exists.** `PruneStmt ::= 'prune' QName` (`railroad.md:396`) takes a schema object; `evolution.md:186` is `prune Customer`, a whole table. "Orphaned branch" is defined at `transaction-graph.md:88-92` as *a transaction-graph branch never merged to `main`* — not a row whose inbound FK count hit zero. `documents.md:216`'s "prunable once no live row references it" is about a generated **key table**, again a schema object. There is no `where` on `PruneStmt`, no row identifier in the production, and no refcount anywhere. So §3's bolded thesis — "Content addressing is what converts 'append-only forever' into the already-solved orphan-prune problem" — is false: the already-solved problem is schema-object pruning and unmerged branches, neither of which is a superseded content row. Everything downstream fails with it: §7's "bounded to the retention window on old `Deploy` rows once orphan-prune runs", §8's "Orphan-prune is the workhorse", and the cost table's "one copy per distinct digest per shard root". As written, a `UserData` blob table grows without bound forever.

- **`Content`'s version chain is not length 1, and nothing in the language makes it so.** §3 claims "Its key is its content, so it can never be updated, only inserted... This is what *earns* the prune: there is no history to destroy." But `Update ::= Query RecordLit` (`railroad.md:637`) applies to any row, and append-only is a **`LogData`** property — `traits.md:304`: "Every field other than the `QueueState` field is append-only, as `LogData` requires." `UserData` has no such rule and there is no `Immutable` trait. `app.web.Content where site == s && ... { media = Css }` produces version 2 today. Worse, `{ body = <new octets> }` is grammatical and leaves `body.digest` disagreeing with the `unique contentRef` entry that keyed on the old digest. The design needs an insert-only enforcement it never proposes.

- **Component ordinals are per-parent, start at 1, and are never reused — so `B / chunk_size` is never the chunk's `ordinal`.** `transaction-graph.md:487-488`: "Ordinals are assigned per parent, monotonically, starting at 1, and are never reused." The proposal flags only the adjacent per-field-namespace question and then builds on the assumption it resolves favorably. Three properties break it outright: (a) chunks begin at parent-max+1, not 0; (b) any other component under the same parent — a `Settings : Component`, a second `Blob`, a `Doc indexed` node tree — draws from the same counter and interleaves; (c) "never reused" means rewriting the field appends at higher ordinals and burns the old ones, so the base moves per version. §6's `lo = a / chunk_size, hi = b / chunk_size` and §2's "the chunk index is **already a column** — `ordinal`" both require a dense, zero-based, per-field index that does not exist. Fixing it needs a stored per-version base, which is new state the proposal doesn't propose — and O(1) byte-offset→ordinal is the *entire* stated reason for rejecting content-defined chunking in §2, so that rejection loses its argument too. Separately, `traits.md:224`'s 2^32-per-parent cap under never-reuse is a *rewrite* budget, not a size budget, so "4 EiB at 1 MiB chunks. Non-issue" is the wrong reading of the limit.

- **Dedup breaks `erase`, which the proposal claims is free.** `interactions` says "`erase` on a `Personal` table cascades to the blob through the FK chain for free (integrity.md:386-388)". That citation says erasing a **shard root** cascades because every dependent reaches the root — which is a different act. In §3's schema `Content` is a dependent of `Site`, not of the `Personal` row, so `erase app.crm.Contact <id>` never reaches a `Content` keyed `{site, body.digest}`: the attachment's octets survive the erasure that closed the person's history. And if the FK were rearranged so it *did* reach, dedup makes the payload shared — erasing user A destroys user B's byte-identical attachment, and `erase` has no last-referrer semantics anywhere in the docs. The proposal names this exact hazard for `scrub` ("destroys it for every referring row") and then asserts erase is free. This is the load-bearing case: §7 says `Blob` is *for* "user uploads... anything whose provenance and access control are the point."

- **Dedup collapses N access policies into one row, and reintroduces the Harnik confirmation oracle one scope in.** §3 scopes dedup per shard root on the side-channel argument. But a shard root is a *tenant*, and tenants have users. One `Content` row referenced by N users' `Asset` rows carries exactly one `assert`, evaluated on itself, and `Content`'s own fields are only `site`, `media`, `body` — nothing identifying an owner. To make it readable by the right people you must write an assert reaching back along the reverse `Asset.content` edge, which `railroad.md:253-254` permits ("in either direction") and which asserts non-empty — i.e. "readable if *any* referring asset is accessible to me." That is the same oracle: upload a file, see whether it reads back, learn whether a colleague already has it. Even without the assert, the `unique` failure on insert and storage accounting leak it. The scoping decision answers the cross-tenant case and manufactures the intra-tenant one, which is where multi-user tenants actually live.

**Corrections**

- **The strongest critique the proposal never engages: the language already expresses this, today, with no new type.** `tables.md:414-433` gives inline `Component` sub-tables. Write `table app.web.Content : UserData { site :> Site, digest : Bytes, length : Int, chunks :> ContentChunk : Component { bytes : Bytes }, unique contentRef { site, digest } }` and you get every one of §2's five table-row properties — one contiguous range scan (`storage.md:41-51`), a zero-byte parent link (`transaction-graph.md:483-485`), containment clustering (`storage.md:120-134`), `ordinal` (`tables.md:43-47`), cascade delete (`tables.md:461-464`) — plus a **real** `digest` column that is key-eligible by ordinary rules rather than by a new virtual-column clause. Note what disappears with it: because each chunk's `bytes` is bounded by `chunk_size`, `unique`, `==`, `order by`, and `where` over it all stay meaningful and cheap. **`Blob` manufactures the unbounded scalar whose eight new constraint bullets then exist to forbid.** `alternatives_rejected` lists this shape and says "This is what the design does" — conflating a hand-written spelling with a new primitive, and so never asking whether the primitive is needed.

- **The trait rejection is too quick.** `alternatives_rejected` #10 rejects a trait because "modelling it as a table shape would make every asset table hand-roll reassembly, digesting, length, and range reads." But `TraitItem ::= FieldDecl | FunctionDecl | EventDecl | UiHint` (`railroad.md:214`) — a trait carries exactly those functions, and `traits.md:419-441` is the standing precedent for a trait supplying a computed value together with the fields it closes over (that is why `Behavior` lives in a trait rather than a type). A `trait Chunked` supplying `digest`, `length`, the chunk component, and the reassembly/range functions is a strictly cheaper answer than a primitive plus eight grammar bullets.

- **§7's `diff` argument is wrong given the key it declares.** `AssetRef` is keyed `unique assetRefKey { deploy, path }`. `diff` "returns the query's rows keyed by their derived key" (`open-questions.md:397`, `railroad.md:686-690`), so v9's rows and v10's rows have **different keys** — a diff across two graph points reports every v10 row as an addition and nothing as `change`. Also `DiffClause`'s two `StringLit`s are graph version tokens, never application deploy names. The recommendation is right; this support for it isn't. Key a current-assets table `{ site, path }` and diff the two commits that deployed, or drop the argument.

- **Head-of-line blocking is the dominant scale failure and appears nowhere.** The shard primary linearizes writes (`transaction-graph.md:489-490`) and synchronous durability waits for both secondaries before commit (`distribution.md:104, 113-116`), and §9 insists one blob write is one transaction and one frame. So a `max_blob_bytes` of 64–256 MiB means one upload stalls **every other write to that tenant's shard** for a 128–512 MiB fan-out. Dedup is scoped per tenant precisely so the blob is shard-local, which is exactly what puts it in the way of that tenant's `Order` inserts. This argues the recommended `max_blob_bytes` is an order of magnitude too high, and it belongs in §4's failure table and the cost table.

- **`Encrypted Blob` is underspecified in a way that is either a compile error or a leak.** `types.md:496-499`: `Encrypted` inherits every `Secret` restriction and `unique`/`indexed`/`order by` are rejected because "the constraint or arrangement would be over ciphertext and could not mean what it says." The proposal admits `Encrypted Blob` while keeping `unique { site, body.digest }`. If `digest` is over plaintext, that `unique` is a deterministic-equality oracle over sealed values — the channel `types.md:387-389` removed `==` to close. If over ciphertext, dedup never fires. Separately `body.length` on an `Encrypted Blob` publishes the plaintext length to every token, which `types.md:371` ("Never to the stored bytes, for any token") never contemplated. Pick one and write the rule.

- **§10 creates a real `Doc`/`Blob` path collision and reintroduces the write amplification `Doc` exists to avoid.** `documents.md:235-243` resolves `body.<key>` through the shredded tree. Give `body : Doc indexed` a payload `{"length": 42, "digest": "..."}` that exceeds `chunk_size` and `body.length` names both the document key and the octet count. Separately, `documents.md:46-48` gives write amplification as reason 2 for keeping bytes in the row — "a 200-key payload shreds into 200 rows in one transaction's mutation list. On a log or ingest path that is the hot path" — and chunking puts N component rows back into that mutation list on exactly that path. "Nothing semantic changes" is not free. Also state that HMAC verification runs on the inbound bytes at the connector boundary, not on the stored chunks, or §6's Effect-only rule makes webhooks commit before they authenticate.

- **Scrub permanently poisons the digest slot with no release path.** After `scrub app.web.Content.body at seq N` the octets are gone but the row and its `unique { site, body.digest }` entry remain — the proposal insists `digest` is not re-derived. A later legitimate upload of the same content now fails the constraint against a row holding no bytes. The escape hatch, `release unique FieldPath StringLit` (`railroad.md:826`), is "rejected where the owning row is neither deleted nor erased" (`railroad.md:840-841`), and a scrubbed row is neither. Add the case or it is unrecoverable.

- **"A rewrite that changes nothing writes nothing" needs an upsert the grammar doesn't have.** `Insert ::= QName RecordLit` (`railroad.md:635`). A duplicate digest is a constraint *violation* — an error the deploy tool must swallow, or a query-then-insert race. `tables.md:143` mentions upsert-by-natural-key for connector ingest but no surface syntax exists.

- **A Haskell reader misreads `Blob` in the one place it matters.** The `Bytes`-is-strict / `Blob`-is-lazy analogy is sold as the argument for two types. But `Data.ByteString.Lazy` is a *pure value* you can `length`, `==`, `splitAt`, and consume. This `Blob` is unreadable in `Pure`, `Read`, and `Tx`, so it is not a lazy `ByteString` — it is an opaque handle, closer to `Handle` or `ForeignPtr`. Advertising the `ByteString.Lazy` shape and then rejecting `==`, `where`, `group`, `order by`, and every eliminator is precisely the mismatch CLAUDE.md's "make it feel like Haskell" tie-breaker exists to prevent. `implementation_notes` already names the honest type — `BlobHandle` — which is what the surface should say. Second misreading: `body : Blob | NotGiven` reads as a sum you can case on; you can't. Third, minor: `length` is already a stdlib function (`types.md:38`, `\z -> length z == 5`), so a Haskell reader writes `length body` while the proposal requires `body.length` and rejects `length body` — two spellings for one number, one of them a compile error.

- **`BlobPolicy` needs two tables, not one with an override.** `transaction-graph.md:333-335` forced `ExtentPolicy` + `ExtentOverride` apart because "a `Null`-derived variant in a key is rejected." §2's "a `system.shards.BlobPolicy` row keyed by table path with a per-server override" glosses the same constraint that the shape it cites was built to satisfy.

- **Grammar delta and reserved words: these parts hold.** I could construct no ambiguous input. `Blob` is an ordinary identifier (`railroad.md:1033-1036`); `body.digest` is an existing `FieldPath` (`railroad.md:28, 219`); the maximal-munch prefix table (`railroad.md:580-592`) is untouched because no operator is added; `--format raw` (`railroad.md:749`) and `scrub FieldPath at seq NumLit` (`railroad.md:825`, though the mandatory `ReasonClause` is omitted from the quote) both exist. None of `blob`, `file`, `asset`, `attachment`, `stream`, `chunk`, `chunked`, `range` appears in `railroad.md:879-893`, and open-questions.md argues against reserving none of them. `Path`, `Format`, and `MediaType` in the examples collide with EBNF nonterminals only, not tokens. OQ-038 is the correct next number (highest existing is OQ-037 at `open-questions.md:298`).

- **Spot-check results — three cited facts are wrong or inverted, out of ~30 checked.** (1) The `retain`-is-`LogData`-only claim, cited to `railroad.md:417-420` and `traits.md:107-111`, is contradicted by `aggregates.md:322`. **Wrong.** (2) `railroad.md:958-961` is said to "decline to reserve `next`" — `next` **is** reserved (`railroad.md:886`); those lines explain why reserving it was acceptable. **Backwards**, though the linked-list point survives. (3) `storage.md:186` is cited for "the Cap'n Proto single-segment assumption" of the log frame; line 186 is about schema evolution, and the single-segment phrase at line 183 describes the **replication wire format**, not the frame — so the claim is not doc-backed at all. Also: `railroad.md:417-420` is overread into row-level orphan-prune; `cli.md:297` is five lines off the `--format raw` example; and calling a stored `digest` "the same 'cache rather than projection' status `updated_at` has" inverts `storage.md:98-100`, which makes per-field timestamps a cache *because* they are derivable. Everything else verified correct, including all of `storage.md:13-19/29-30/41-51/77-83/109-113/120-134/146-149`, `documents.md:3/32/41-45/68-81/254`, `traits.md:141-171/175-177/199/220-224/326-330/353/361-368`, `tables.md:36-41/43-47/161-176/213-218/461-464`, `types.md:22/103-114/482-490`, `transaction-graph.md:314-337/475-491`, `distribution.md:113-131/161-170/288-289`, `integrity.md:208/386-388/407/418/422-424`, `auth.md:318/390`, `events.md:504-506`, `open-questions.md:399/400/490-494`, `api.md:52-57`, `api-and-rendering.md:7-12/68/72-76`. The three flagged doc inconsistencies (theme CSS as `Reference`, no octet-stream content type, `Doc`'s unstated ceiling) are all real.

- **Keep §7.** "Store the manifest, not the artifact" is the right call and the `storage.md:146-149` / `traits.md:353` reasoning behind it holds. It needs only the §7 `diff` repair above and an honest §7 number: with F1's `retain` chain the 14 GB/year figure is bounded as claimed; without it, it is unbounded, and the proposal's own "single-binary exception" was resting on the mechanism that doesn't exist.

**Missed interactions**

- **Erase + dedup**: `erase` on a `Personal` row never reaches a site-rooted `Content` row, and if it did it would destroy another user's identical payload. No last-referrer semantics exist. (fatal #5)

- **Access asserts + dedup**: one `Content` row, N owners, one assert — an intra-tenant confirmation oracle, and no way to express per-referrer readability without asserting non-empty over the reverse edge. (fatal #6)

- **Head-of-line blocking**: `transaction-graph.md:489-490` linearizes shard writes and `distribution.md:104` blocks the commit on two ACKs, so one 128 MiB upload stalls every other write to that tenant's shard.

- **Ordinal read-modify-write cost**: `transaction-graph.md:488` — "The assignment is a read-modify-write against the parent's current maximum." A 1 GB blob at 1 MiB chunks is 1 024 sequential RMWs against one parent inside one transaction.

- **Scrub + `unique` with no `release`**: `railroad.md:840-841` rejects `release` on a row that is neither deleted nor erased, and a scrubbed row is neither, so the poisoned digest slot is permanent.

- **Thick clients**: `api-and-rendering.md:109-115` — a thick client "holds a local replica of the schema and data (within its access scope)" and consumes the binary replication protocol. §5 covers subscribed *clients* getting invalidation only, but a thick-client replica pulls every payload in scope. Unaddressed.

- **`verify shard deep` and `export`/`import shard`** (`railroad.md:866-869`): a 1 024-chunk blob's cost in deep verification and in shard export/import is unbudgeted anywhere in §4.

- **`retain` branch predicates are decidable at write time** (`railroad.md:382`, `aggregates.md:306-307`: "a branch predicate may reference only group keys and the time source, so the branch is decidable when the row is written"). So the fix in fatal #1 can key on `created_at`/`site` but not on "superseded" — state that when writing the chain, and use the two-step `for N day, drop` form which `aggregates.md:164-170` confirms needs no `as` binding.

- **Insert-only enforcement has no home.** The one append-only rule in the language is `LogData`'s (`traits.md:304`) and its single exemption is the `QueueState` field. Making `Content` genuinely immutable is a new rule that needs a normative home, or the design should stop claiming version-chain length 1.

**Simpler alternative**

Add no primitive type. Ship a standard-library trait plus one HTTP mode, and use the discard path that already exists.

```
trait Chunked {
  digest : Bytes,          -- declared, not virtual; key-eligible by the ordinary rule
  length : Int,
  chunks :> Chunk : Component { seq : Int, bytes : Bytes }
}

table app.web.Content : UserData, Chunked {
  site  :> Site,
  media :> MediaType,
  unique contentRef { site, digest }
}

retain app.web.Content
  for 90 day
  , drop
```

Why this gets 90% for a fraction of the cost:

- **Zero new primitives, zero new virtual columns, zero constraint bullets.** Every rejection the proposal needs (`unique`, `==`, `group`, `order by`, `where`-scope) is unnecessary, because `bytes` is bounded by `chunk_size`. The proposal's rule list exists only to contain a problem it created.
- **The discard path is real and already written.** `aggregates.md:164-170` is the no-binding chain form; `aggregates.md:322-353` confirms `retain` on `UserData`; `aggregates.md:377-379` confirms the `Component` subtree prunes with its parent. No orphan detection, no refcount, no invented mechanism — and it keeps "discarding is never manual" and "silence means keep" intact.
- **A declared `digest` beats a virtual one.** `unique`, `==`, `order by`, key membership, and `diff` all just work on it under existing rules, and `distribution.md:288-289` already makes the index hold a digest of it.
- **An explicit `seq : Int` on the chunk row costs four bytes and buys correct O(1) offset arithmetic**, immune to the per-parent / start-at-1 / never-reused ordinal problem (fatal #4). This is the concrete reason declaring the chunk table beats generating it.
- **What genuinely remains is implementation, not language**: a `system.api.FormatFunctor` row (`api.md:52-57`) that streams a chunk range with `ETag` = `digest`, `Content-Length` = `length`, `Accept-Ranges`, `Range` → `seq` arithmetic, and a `304` short-circuit before any chunk read; plus a driver-side chunker that accumulates the digest streaming. Both stay inside the self-hosting story, which is where the proposal correctly wanted them.
- **If ergonomics later justify sugar, it is `Bytes chunked`, parallel to `Doc indexed`** — and the proposal's own reason for rejecting it ("chunk size tracks hardware, so it is a `Configuration` row") is an argument against putting the *number* in the clause, not against the clause. `indexed` names no cap either.

Keep §7 unchanged: store the manifest, not the artifact, with the `diff` argument repaired per the correction above. Keep the `MediaType : Reference, Extensible` table, the `nosniff` / `Content-Disposition` / separate-origin policy, the immutable digest-addressed URL, and the durability-class split — those parts are right and cost nothing. Drop cluster-scoped dedup, and treat per-tenant dedup as opt-in per table rather than baked into the design, because of fatal objections 5 and 6.

### Questions for you

- Is the target deployment single-binary and CDN-free? That is the one condition under which I would reverse the frontend-artifact recommendation, and it changes nothing else in the design — you use the same `Blob` and the same content addressing, you just accept the orphan-prune loop as the discard path.
- Should `Blob` be readable at all inside a `Read` functor, or is `Effect`-only correct? I have it as `Effect`-only on the transparency argument, but a bounded read of the first N bytes (magic-number validation, image dimensions) is a plausible thing to want and would need a `body.prefix n : Bytes` projection. Adding it later is cheap; deciding now is cheaper.
- Do you want the per-field ordinal-space question resolved in this pass, or as its own item? It is already ambiguous today for a table with two `Doc indexed` fields, so `Blob` exposes it rather than creating it — but it becomes load-bearing the moment a table has two `Blob` fields.
- Is per-shard-root dedup the right scope, or do you want a knob for cluster-wide? I have it fixed at per-root on placement and side-channel grounds. Making it configurable would need the content table's key to vary, which is not a `Configuration` row's job.
- Should `MediaType` ship as a `system.*` `Reference, Extensible` table, or is it the application's to declare? Shipping it means DataCode owns an IANA mirror; not shipping it means every schema re-declares one.
- Anything else you want folded in — a size target, an existing asset pipeline this has to interoperate with, or a case (streaming video, resumable upload, signed URLs) you have in mind that I have not covered?
- (from the critic) Do you want dedup at all in v1? Fatal objections 5 and 6 say the `unique { root, digest }` pattern breaks `erase` and collapses N access policies onto one row. Making dedup an opt-in the author writes per table (rather than the design's spine) keeps the storage win where it is safe — first-party build artifacts, one owner — and keeps it away from `Personal` uploads where it is a correctness and privacy bug.
- (from the critic) Is there a case for an `Immutable` marker trait? Fatal #3 shows `Content`'s insert-only property is assumed and unenforced, and `traits.md:304` puts the only append-only rule on `LogData`. `Immutable` composing like `Keyless` and `Personal` would make it structural, and it would also let `Content` state that `body` is never updated so the `unique` index can never disagree with the stored digest.
- (from the critic) Should the chunk table carry an explicit `seq : Int` rather than leaning on `ordinal`? I recommend yes (four bytes, correct O(1) offset arithmetic, immune to the per-parent ordinal question). Saying yes also settles whether the per-(parent, component-table) ordinal namespace question needs answering at all for this feature — it wouldn't.
- (from the critic) What is the real `max_blob_bytes` target, given head-of-line blocking? 64–256 MiB on a synchronously-replicated, linearized shard primary means one upload stalls a tenant's whole write path for a 128–512 MiB fan-out. If uploads must be large, the honest answer may be a `Batched` durability class plus a smaller ceiling, not a bigger one.
- (from the critic) Anything else you want folded in — a size target, a specific upload path (resumable, signed URL, streaming video), an existing asset pipeline this has to interoperate with, or a tenancy shape (single-user vs multi-user per shard root) that would change the dedup and access answers?

---

## D02-bounded-text

**Designer verdict:** reject-with-alternative · **Critic verdict:** sound-with-corrections

### Headline

No grammar change and no new type: a length cap is a validation predicate, and `where maxLen 255` / `where minLen 1` already exist and are already used in five documents. Reject `Text 255` / `Text 1 255` — arity overloading makes the first number mean two things, a type argument has no address for `enforce`/`monitor`/`repair`, and a type-level cap makes over-length connector data untypeable, which halts a binlog instead of recording a violation.

### Pushback

Three things are wrong with the request as stated.

**1. The feature already exists, with a spelling the docs use.** `maxLen` and `minLen` appear as `where` predicates in `docs/schema/README.md:217,241`, `docs/schema/types.md:52,399`, `docs/schema/tables.md:94`, `docs/schema/evolution.md:94`, `docs/schema/traits.md:60`, and `docs/auth.md:69`. `Text 255` would be a second spelling for a rule that has one — the defect OQ-005 keeps withdrawing things for (`rename from`, `delete!`, postfix aggregates, `split`/`merge`). What is genuinely missing is not syntax; it is that `maxLen` is used eight times and *defined nowhere*, and that "255 characters" has never been pinned to a counting unit.

**2. "Same type, two constructors" is not a Haskell shape.** A Haskell type constructor has one fixed arity. You cannot have `Text :: Nat -> Type` and `Text :: Nat -> Nat -> Type` simultaneously; what the request describes is arity overloading on one constructor, and the Haskell-legal encoding is `Text (Max 255)` / `Text (Range 1 255)` — longer than the predicate it would replace. It fails the tie-breaker in `CLAUDE.md`.

Worse, the first number would change meaning based on whether a second follows: `Text 10` caps at 10, `Text 10 200` floors at 10. Adjacent lines in a field list would read differently for the same token. That is the same defect OQ-005 recorded when it withdrew the `days` conversion family — "one name was bound twice" (`open-questions.md:375`) — one position over.

**3. It would break connector ingest.** `integrity.md:92-101` requires that a rule over connector-sourced data default to `monitor`, because "a MariaDB binlog stream whose commit fails stops at that offset and never advances". A `VARCHAR(255)` source column that emits 300 characters — after a source `ALTER`, or under a relaxed `sql_mode` — must land as a recorded violation. A predicate can be `monitor`ed. A **type** cannot: an over-length value is simply untypeable, the commit fails, and the connector halts. This is the argument that decides it on its own.

A fourth, smaller point: `TypeArg ::= QName | Literal` (`railroad.md:96`) is a single token with no parenthesized alternative, so `Hashed Text 255` parses as `Hashed` applied to *three* arguments, not `Hashed (Text 255)`. Adopting the form would require adding `TypeArg ::= … | '(' TypeExpr ')'` for one type's benefit, and `type Password : Hashed (Text 12 64) using …` would then sit beside `where minLen 12` doing the same job (`auth.md:69`).

### Recommendation

## Answer to the question as asked

**Neither.** Not one type with two constructors, and not a user-defined type *per case*. A length cap is a **validation predicate** applied in a `where` block, and the reusable unit is a **named domain type** declared once per meaning.

```
-- one-off
note : Text where maxLen 500

-- the "two numbers" case, each number labelled
username : Text
  where
    minLen 3
    maxLen 32

-- the reusable case: name the concept, declare the cap once
type PersonName : Text where maxLen 100
type Slug       : Text where
                    minLen 1
                    maxLen 64
                    \s -> s =~ "^[a-z0-9-]+$"
```

`Text 255` is *already grammatical* under `Variant ::= QName TypeArg*` / `TypeArg ::= QName | Literal` (`railroad.md:94-96`). No type in DataCode takes a literal argument today — `Hashed Text using <QName>`, `Encrypted Text using <QName>`, `Behavior Amount`, `Doc` are all the whole set — so the `Literal` alternative has no user. Keep it, and give it one: `name : Text 255` should **parse and be rejected at name resolution** with `where maxLen 255` in the diagnostic. That is a better error than a parse failure at `255`, and it is the spelling every SQL author will try first.

## Why a predicate and not a type argument

### The discriminator, stated once

> **A type argument is warranted when it changes the representation or the set of admissible operations. A `where` predicate is warranted when it only narrows the value set.**

`Hashed Text` changes both — the stored bytes become a digest and `==` becomes a compile error (`types.md:361-395`). `Encrypted Text` changes both. `Behavior a` changes read semantics. `Text 255` changes neither.

The language has already answered the identical question for numbers and did it this way: `Decimal` is **arbitrary-precision** (`types.md:14`) and its scale is a predicate — `isRoundedToCents` in `CLAUDE.md`'s quick reference, `\a -> a >= 0` in `types.md:37`. There is no `Decimal 12 2`. Text should not diverge.

OQ-005 also already rejected the neighbouring move: `type Day : Duration` was refused partly because "`type X : Y` is a transparent refinement with no constructor, so there is nothing to apply" (`open-questions.md:375`).

### The cap has no address, and it needs one

`ValidationRef ::= QName ( '/' Ident )?` (`railroad.md:431`). Every enforcement mode — `enforce always`, `enforce forward`, `monitor`, `repair … into` — addresses a predicate by the function it applies. A type argument is not a predicate and has no `Ident` to select.

This is not theoretical. `integrity.md:173-197` makes a mode **mandatory** when a predicate is added to a populated field, and the mechanism is the report:

```
error: app.auth.User.username / maxLen is new and app.auth.User has 41 208 rows.
       1 284 rows (3.1%) do not satisfy it.
       State a mode in this transaction:
         enforce app.auth.User.username / maxLen always
         enforce app.auth.User.username / maxLen forward
         monitor app.auth.User.username / maxLen
```

Under `Text 255` → `Text 100` there is nothing to name on the right of the `/`. You would have to invent an address for the type argument — that is, reinvent the predicate, having paid for a grammar change to avoid it.

### The cap is not physical, so nothing is bought

| Consumer | What a declared cap buys |
|---|---|
| Log bytes on disk | **Nothing.** Cap'n Proto `Text` is a pointer to a variable-length UTF-8 blob (`storage.md:8-23`); `log_index` records `{offset, length}` per *row version*, not per field (`storage.md:29,63`). There is no fixed-width text to allocate. |
| `unique` index | **Nothing.** The index stores a keyed digest, never the value, and partitions on the digest (`distribution.md:288`). Digests are fixed width already. |
| Cross-shard traffic | **Nothing.** |
| Commit cost | One `Data.Text.length` per field per write — negligible against a ~0.15 µs/tx encode at 10 mutations (`storage.md:18-19`). |
| Read cost | **Zero.** Validations do not run on read; only access asserts do (`integrity.md:348`). |

There is exactly one place a Text bound has physical bite: an LMDB arrangement keyed on a Text column, against LMDB's 511-byte key limit. That is not a reason to declare a cap, because **materialization is automatic and operator-overridable, not the schema author's decision** (`storage.md` "Materialization", OQ-005 bullet at `open-questions.md:388`). The planner digests or prefix-truncates an over-long arrangement key with a stored tiebreak; the schema says nothing about it.

### The number is already statically available

Functors are interpreted DSL terms precisely so that "the optimizer, static access analysis, coercion-path derivation, and the IDE all consume their STRUCTURE" (OQ-001). A `maxLen 254` term carries the literal `254` as a node. Every consumer that wants the cap statically — connector column mapping, UI field width, API/JSON-schema export, `:describe`, the IDE — reads it off the schema graph walk it already performs. Encoding the cap in the type would supply the same number by a second route, which is the redundancy the project treats as a defect.

## Counting: code points, and why

> **`Text` length is counted in Unicode scalar values (code points). `maxLen`, `minLen`, and `length` all mean the same thing by it.**

This is already the de facto rule: `Data.Text` is auto-available (`functions.md:116-117`), `types.md:38` writes `\z -> length z == 5`, and `Data.Text.length` counts `Char`, which is a code point.

Three reasons to fix it there:

- **MariaDB round trip is exact.** MySQL/MariaDB count `CHAR`/`VARCHAR` lengths in *characters* under a multibyte charset, and `utf8mb4` covers all of Unicode at ≤4 bytes per character. `VARCHAR(255)` is therefore 255 code points, and a shadow-schema mapping to `where maxLen 255` is lossless in both directions. Byte counting would silently reject valid source rows.
- **Grapheme clusters are non-deterministic across servers.** UAX #29 grapheme-cluster boundaries are revised between Unicode versions, so a grapheme count depends on the ICU build on the evaluating server. `integrity.md:16-41` makes conformance a function of `(row, functor address, schema node)`; a grapheme count would add a hidden fourth parameter, two replicas could disagree, and a materialized-view refresh on an upgraded server could flip a violation on and off with no commit. This is the **same recomputation-determinism rule that bans clock reads inside a functor** (`functions.md:119-134`), not a new one — which is the right way to refuse it.
- **Byte length is still wanted sometimes**, so give it its own name rather than overloading one.

```
minLen   : Int -> Text -> Bool     -- code points, inclusive
maxLen   : Int -> Text -> Bool     -- code points, inclusive
maxBytes : Int -> Text -> Bool     -- UTF-8 bytes, for a byte-limited external column or wire field
```

Currying is what makes this work with no special form: `maxLen 254` is a `Text -> Bool`, which is exactly what a `where` block takes and auto-lifts (`functions.md:74-80`, `types.md:64-66`). "Make it feel like Haskell" lands on the existing answer.

### Consequences to state explicitly

- **No implicit trimming.** `maxLen` counts what is stored, trailing whitespace included. DataCode stores what it was given. Offer `isTrimmed` as a predicate; never trim silently.
- **No implicit normalization.** `é` is one code point in NFC and two in NFD, so a client sending NFD gets a different count. Normalization is an explicit predicate (`isNfc`) or a migration function (`toNfc`) applied in a projection, never a hidden rewrite.
- **A `utf8mb3` source column is a charset violation, not a length one.** A shadow field over `utf8mb3` cannot hold non-BMP text at all; the connector records that as its own `Forced` violation rather than folding it into a cap.

## Edge cases

| Case | Rule |
|---|---|
| `maxLen 0` | Legal; means "empty only". Odd, not wrong. |
| `maxLen (-1)`, or `minLen 10` with `maxLen 5` in one block | **Unsatisfiable by construction; rejected at schema commit.** Both arguments are literals, so the check is free, and the language already refuses unsatisfiable-by-construction declarations elsewhere (`IsoWeek → Month`, `types.md:255-274`). |
| Two `maxLen` in one `where` block | Rejected as redundant — their conjunction is the tighter one, so write it. |
| Two `maxLen` arriving from different traits | Both enforced, both live, distinguished by origin path (`A.name / maxLen`, `B.name / maxLen`). This is the existing rule at `README.md:282-294`, unchanged. |
| `maxLen` on a `Hashed`/`Encrypted` field | Admissible — it is `a -> Bool`, the only signature a `Secret` type accepts (`types.md:371-374`). `auth.md:69` already does this. A violation reports `observed = Redacted` (`integrity.md:267-276`). |
| `maxLen` on `Doc`, `Behavior`, a function type, `Bytes` | Type error, or already rejected by the existing `where`-rejection rules (`railroad.md:168-176`). No new rule needed. |
| Empty string versus absence | Orthogonal. `''` is a `Text`; absence is `Text \| NotGiven`. `minLen 1` says nothing about which. |
| Field-level `where` on an alternation | A `Text -> Bool` predicate on `nickname : Nickname \| NotGiven` applies at the variants it is well-typed at and is vacuously true at the `Null`-derived ones. This is an adjacent hole bounded text makes common — see the questions below. |

## Subtyping and cap accumulation

`Text 10` versus `Text 255` needs no variance rule, because **conjunction already is the subtyping**. A field declared `email : Email` mints a field-scoped subtype at `namespace.table.field` and inherits `Email`'s predicates, extending them (`types.md:69-71`, `category-model.md:181`); a field merged from two traits carries both traits' predicates (`traits.md:73-88`). So:

```
type Email : Text where
               isValidEmail
               maxLen 254

table app.commerce.Customer {
  email : Email unique where maxLen 100      -- effective cap: 100
}
```

Both predicates hold, so the effective cap is the minimum, and it is **monotone in the tightening direction only**. Declaring `maxLen 300` on that field does not widen anything — `Email`'s 254 still applies — which is the correct answer and the one you get for free.

A type-argument spelling would invite the opposite reading. `email : Text 300` over `type Email : Text 254` looks like an override, and making it *not* one requires a variance rule nobody asked for. That is a semantic trap the predicate form does not have.

## Redeclaring `maxLen 255` → `maxLen 100`

Under `evolution.md:81-119` the field is redeclared with the `where` block you want and the diff is taken per address. One rule needs stating, because bounded text makes it common:

> **A predicate's address is the function it applies; its arguments are part of its definition, not its address.**

So `maxLen 254` → `maxLen 100` is a *change to* `app.commerce.Customer.email / maxLen`, not a new predicate beside it. And the mode rule reduces to the blast-radius query that `integrity.md:178` already runs: **state a mode iff any existing row stops conforming.** That subsumes `evolution.md:118`'s "relaxing or removing a predicate needs no mode" as the zero case, so tightening 255→100 demands a mode and loosening 100→255 does not, with no new machinery and no direction analysis.

Nothing is rewritten. Rows committed under the old node stay conforming *at that node* (`integrity.md:16-41`); the tightened cap is a fact about them relative to HEAD. `enforce forward` grandfathers them; `monitor` records only.

**Adjacent inconsistency, flagged not fixed:** `integrity.md:141-143,187-189`, `cli.md:235,252`, `evolution.md:110`, and `railroad.md:441` all write `/ minLen12`, but `README.md:300-302` says "a predicate is identified by the function it applies". Those four files should read `/ minLen`. It is a design decision (does the address include the argument?) so I am not applying it unilaterally, but the answer above settles it and the files disagree with themselves today.

## Do not ship size-named types

Resist a standard library of `Text32` / `Text64` / `Text255`. A name that is only a number is the number with extra steps, it becomes the default everyone reaches for, and the cap stops meaning anything. Name the concept:

```
type PersonName  : Text where maxLen 100
type UrlPath     : Text where maxLen 2048
type CountryCode : Text where
                     minLen 2
                     maxLen 2
```

If a project genuinely wants size-graded types, it declares them in its own namespace (`app.text.Short`), where they are that project's decision and not the language's.

For "most `Text` fields need a cap", the lever is a **linter warning on an uncapped `Text` field**, not a default value. A default cap nobody chose would appear in every schema and be wrong somewhere; a warning gets the cap written where it belongs, and it is the same never-silent posture the degenerate-derived-key rule takes (`open-questions.md:379`).

## Generalising to `Int 0 100`

Same answer, same reasons, and the language already committed to it: `type Amount : Decimal where \a -> a >= 0` (`types.md:37`) and `isRoundedToCents` (`CLAUDE.md`). Write a named domain type or an inline predicate:

```
type Percent : Int where \n -> n >= 0 && n <= 100
```

The discriminator above is what keeps this from being ad hoc: a hypothetical `Decimal p s` *would* qualify, because fixed-point precision and scale change the representation. DataCode does not need it — `Decimal` is arbitrary-precision by declaration — but the rule says why the two cases differ rather than treating them as the same request twice.

## Rejected: fusing the two bounds

`lenBetween 1 255` was considered and is **not** recommended. Two separate predicates give two separate addresses, and the two bounds routinely want different enforcement modes — a tightened maximum on legacy imports goes to `monitor` while the minimum stays `enforce always`. One fused predicate has one address and forces one mode on both. That is the direct answer to "one type that takes two numbers": the two numbers want to be two independently-governed rules.

### Grammar delta (per-item; see integrated version before applying)

**No production changes. No new reserved words.** `Text 255` and `Text 1 255` are already grammatical under the existing `Variant ::= QName TypeArg*` / `TypeArg ::= QName | Literal` (`railroad.md:94-96`), and the recommendation is that they be *rejected at name resolution* rather than admitted or made unparseable. `railroad.md` gains three bullets and one reserved-words note.

Add to the "Constraints not expressible in the grammar" list under **## Types** (`railroad.md:104-126`, after the `UsingClause` paragraph):

```
- **No type constructor takes a `Literal` argument.** The `Literal` alternative in `TypeArg`
  has no user and exists so that `name : Text 255` — the spelling a SQL author reaches for —
  parses and is rejected at name resolution with `where maxLen 255` in the diagnostic, rather
  than failing as a parse error at `255`. A length cap narrows a value set; it does not change
  a representation, so it is a validation. See
  [types.md](types.md#length-is-a-predicate-not-a-type-argument).

- **A `TypeArg` is a single token**, so a parameterised type cannot be an argument to another:
  `Hashed Text 255` is `Hashed` applied to three arguments, not `Hashed (Text 255)`. This is the
  second reason literal type arguments are not admitted — giving `Text` one would require
  `TypeArg ::= QName | Literal | '(' TypeExpr ')'` for `Hashed`'s sake alone, and
  `type Password : Hashed (Text 12 64) using …` would sit beside the `where minLen 12` that
  already does the job.
```

Add to the "Constraints not expressible in the grammar" list under **## Enforcement Modes** (`railroad.md:456-458`):

```
- A `ValidationRef`'s `/ Ident` names the **function a predicate applies**, not the predicate
  plus its arguments: `where maxLen 254` is addressed `… / maxLen`. Changing an argument is a
  change to that predicate, so the mode rule is the blast-radius query — state a mode iff an
  existing row stops conforming. Two applications of one function in a single `where` block are
  rejected as redundant; two arriving from different traits are distinguished by origin path.
```

Also correct the example at `railroad.md:441` from `enforce app.auth.User.username / minLen12 forward` to `enforce app.auth.User.username / minLen forward`.

Add under **## Reserved Words**, in the "considered and deliberately **not** reserved" list:

```
- **`maxLen`, `minLen`, `maxBytes`**, as length-cap keywords or modifiers, and **`varchar`** /
  **`char`** as bounded-text type names. The three predicates are ordinary standard-library
  functions, exactly as `count`, `sum`, and `matches` are, so a user-defined length rule
  (`maxLenAfterTrim`, `maxLinesOf`) is admissible wherever the built-in ones are and needs no
  grammar entry. Reserving them would make a length cap a language feature rather than a library
  one, which is what forced the closed `Aggregate` production to be withdrawn.
```
