## D16-backreference

**Designer verdict:** adopt-with-changes · **Critic verdict:** flawed

### Headline

Adopt the construct, spell it `:<` (not `<:`), and make the left-hand name a real addressable reverse relation rather than throwaway sugar. `:<` mirrors `:>` inside the `:` munch family, avoids the subtyping misread that `<:` guarantees, and reuses `NameClause`'s exact shape (`name :< Child : Trait via fk { … }`) so it costs zero reserved words. `Doc` stays a distinct declaration and gains the nested rendering.

### Pushback

Five things are wrong or under-specified in the request as stated.

**1. `<:` is the subtyping operator, and DataCode's `:` already means subtype.** `type Email : Text` *is* `Email <: Text`. Writing `comments <: Comment` would tell a type-literate reader "comments is a subtype of Comment" — the wrong relation, in a language whose `:` already carries the right one. Scala, F<:, Julia, Ceylon, and PVS all read it that way. Use `:<`.

**2. "The current table does not retain the field; it is just syntactic sugar" under-sells it and makes the left-hand name pointless.** If the LHS names nothing, the honest spelling is a bare table name with a body and no LHS at all — which is unparseable, because capitalization is style and not grammar (`docs/schema/railroad.md:41-46`; OQ-005, `docs/open-questions.md:391`), so the parser cannot tell `Comment { … }` from a field named `Comment`. The LHS has to exist. Given that, make it earn its place: name the reverse relation, and make it addressable. That converts sugar into the one genuinely missing navigation feature and pays a debt the language already has (below).

**3. The two-shard-root claim is wrong in mechanism.** What forces a child out of `Component` is *two owners*, not two shards. `docs/schema/traits.md:222` says "A component may reference outward freely" and an outbound FK crossing a shard is a warning naming the edge, not an error (OQ-005, `docs/open-questions.md:362`). So a linking table referencing two roots *can* be a `Component` of one of them, with the zero-byte parent link intact and a cross-shard FK to the other. The head rule already places it (`docs/schema/tables.md:176-177`). Nothing new is needed here.

**4. Nesting must not decide sharding**, or the "view it either way" requirement collapses. Keep placement where it already lives — the child's declared candidate key — so that which end you nested under is presentational and the flat form round-trips.

**5. Terminology.** `Doc` is a *type*, `indexed` is the storage hint, and `DocKeys` is the trait (`docs/schema/documents.md:34-38, 115-118`). There is no "Doc trait". Also, the generated `…Node` table is not a linking table; it is a component subtree keyed by ordinal nesting, with no stored parent pointer at all (`docs/schema/documents.md:99-106`).

**And one thing the request is exactly right about, with better evidence than it gives.** `docs/schema/tables.md:421-429` declares `headers :> RequestHeader : Component { name : Text, value : Text }`. The field is plural and the example reads as many headers, but `:>` holds *one* reference, so that example means one header per request. The doc's own illustration of component sub-tables is a 1:many shape the language cannot currently write inline. That is the gap.

### Recommendation

# Dependent declarations: `name :< Child`

## The gap

`address :> Address { … }` declares a child inline and puts the FK on the **parent**, so it expresses 1:1 and many:1 only (`docs/schema/tables.md:373-409`). The 1:many shape — order lines, comments, log headers — needs the FK on the **child**, which today forces a second top-level `table` statement and loses the containment reading. `docs/schema/tables.md:421-429` shows the doc tripping over this: `headers :> RequestHeader : Component` reads as many headers and means one.

`group … { rows as Sale : UserData via product }` (`docs/schema/queries.md:215-249`) already generates a sibling table with an FK back to a parent row — but only from a query, never as a stored declaration.

## Spelling

```ebnf
BackRefDecl ::= Ident ':<' QName SubTableTraits? ( 'via' Ident )? SubTableBody?
```

This is `NameClause ::= 'as' Ident ( ':' TraitList )? ( 'via' Ident )?` (`docs/schema/railroad.md:630`) with `:<` in place of `as`, and it does the same three jobs in the same order:

| Part | Effect |
|---|---|
| `comments` | Names the reverse relation on this table |
| `:< Comment` | Names the child table; declares it if new, amends it if not |
| `: Component` | The child's replication trait |
| `via document` | Names the child's FK back; defaults to this table's name in `lower_snake_case` |
| `{ … }` | The child's body |

A reader who knows `rows as Sale : UserData via product` already knows this construct.

```
table app.pm.Document : UserData {
  owner  :> User,
  title   : Text,
  unique docRef { owner, title },

  comments :< Comment : Component {
    body      : Text,
    author   :> User,
    posted_at : Timestamp
  }
}
```

Flat equivalent, which is what the graph stores:

```
table app.pm.Document : UserData {
  owner  :> User,
  title   : Text,
  unique docRef { owner, title },
  comments :< Comment via document        -- bodiless: names the reverse edge only
}

table app.pm.Comment : Component {
  document :> app.pm.Document,            -- the containment link; zero bytes
  body      : Text,
  author   :> User,
  posted_at : Timestamp
}
```

Body optional, exactly as `address :> Address` and `address :> Address { … }` are the same construct at two degrees of completeness (`docs/schema/tables.md:391-409`).

## Why `:<` and not `<:`

**Lexing is not the argument, and overstating it would be wrong.** `:` cannot start an `Atom` (`docs/schema/railroad.md:482-490`), so `a < :b` is not a program and `<:` would in fact lex unambiguously under maximal munch. Three other things decide it:

- **`<:` means the opposite.** Standard subtyping notation, and DataCode's `:` already carries that meaning.
- **Family placement.** `<` and `<=` are live in expression position as `CmpOp`s. `:` and `:>` are not — no expression admits them. Extending the `:` family costs nothing and keeps a mistyped `:<` in a predicate a clear "not a comparison operator" rather than a near-miss inside the comparison family.
- **Haskell reader.** In Haskell an operator beginning with `:` is a data constructor, and `Data.Sequence` pairs `:<` (`ViewL`) with `:>` (`ViewR`) as left-view and right-view. DataCode already took `:>`; `:<` is its partner, pointing the other way, and both read as constructors — which is what they are, building an edge in the schema category.

## Semantics

`comments :< Comment via document` on `app.pm.Document`:

1. **Declares nothing stored on `Document`.**
2. **Declares or amends `app.pm.Comment`**, adding `document :> app.pm.Document`. Namespace defaults to the parent's, as with inline sub-tables; a qualified `QName` places it elsewhere.
3. **Names the reverse relation `Document.comments`** — a table-valued virtual column holding the `Comment` rows whose `document` is this row.
4. The generated FK's **origin address is `app.pm.Document.comments`**, so redeclaring `Comment` cannot drop it. Same rule as a trait-inherited predicate, which is addressed at its trait path and cannot be dropped by redeclaring the table (`docs/schema/evolution.md:98-99`).

### Redeclaration and conflict

Consistent with `docs/schema/evolution.md:10-25`:

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| `Comment` also declared at top level **in the same commit** | Error. Two declarations of one name at one commit point is not a version chain. |
| `Comment` declared in an **earlier** commit, `:<` carries a body | Ordinary redeclaration. Diffs against the current version; `*` behaves as always. |
| `Comment` declared earlier, `:<` bodiless | Amendment adding only the FK, reported in the commit diff. |
| A later top-level `table Comment { … }` omits `document` | Carried forward regardless of `*` — its origin is elsewhere. Drop it with `deprecate app.pm.Document.comments`. |

Names on the right resolve to the version current at the start of the commit; names introduced by the commit resolve within it; the graph must stay acyclic (`docs/schema/evolution.md:15-16`). A `:<` naming a table the same commit introduces is fine under that rule.

**Adding an FK to a populated child.** A bodiless `:<` against an existing populated `Comment` adds a required `:>` with no admissible value for existing rows — a `:>` to a bare table cannot hold `NotFound`. Refuse the commit and name `| MissingDocument` as the fix. This is a pre-existing hole (`docs/schema/evolution.md:274` promises `NotFound` for an added field, which a bare `:>` cannot take); the new construct must not widen it.

### The reverse name is addressable, and that is the point

`Document.comments` is a table-valued column, and the existing rule "a path through a table-valued column distributes to a column" (`docs/schema/queries.md:266-273`) makes the whole query surface fall out with no new production:

```
Document { title, count comments as num_comments }
Document { title, max comments.posted_at as last_activity }
Document where count comments == 0
```

`count :: Table a -> Int` already has the right signature. Aggregate functions are ordinary functions, so nothing is reserved and nothing is special-cased.

It also closes the mandatory-`as` case: `docs/schema/queries.md:134-146` makes `as` mandatory on a reverse join because "the result column has no `:>` field to name it." A named reverse edge supplies one, so `as` becomes optional when the query names the edge.

**Restrictions**, all following from the column being set-valued and unstored:

- **Excluded from `*`.** Otherwise every `Document { * }` drags in every comment. Same reason `Doc` stores bytes and shreds only on `indexed` (`docs/schema/documents.md:41-51`).
- Rejected in a `UniqueDecl`, in `unique`/`indexed` on a field, in `OrderByDecl`, in a `DefaultClause`, and in a `RecordLit`. Add a row to the ineligible-key table in `docs/schema/tables.md:205-212` beside `Doc`, for the same reason: unbounded.
- `: TraitList` on a *projected* reverse column is rejected. The child is a stored table whose trait is declared; a projection may not re-trait it. (`via` and `as` stay available.)
- A `RecordLit` naming a reverse column is a compile-time error. Multi-row nested insert would need a list literal, which the expression grammar does not have and which this proposal does not introduce.

### Component versus dependent

**The trait is declared, not forced by the spelling.** Default is the parent's replication trait — an ordinary dependent. `Component` is opt-in.

Why not default to `Component`: it cascades deletes (`docs/schema/tables.md:461-464`) and forbids outside references (`docs/schema/traits.md:221`). "Nothing is destroyed" is load-bearing; a spelling whose default silently cascades is wrong. It also matches the forward inline sub-table, where `Component` is declared rather than defaulted (`docs/schema/railroad.md:160-162`). `group`'s nested table defaults to `Component` because its rows are already inside the group row; here they are not.

| | `: Component` | Ordinary dependent | Two shard roots |
|---|---|---|---|
| Child identity | parent `DataId` + `Ordinal` | own `DataId` | own `DataId` |
| Parent link on disk | **0 bytes** — the identifier prefix | 12 bytes | 12 bytes |
| Candidate key | exempt | required, must reach the shard root through its FK chain | required; **the first FK in the key decides placement** |
| Placement | parent's shard, by definition | parent's shard, through the key | head FK's shard |
| Lifetime | destroyed with the parent | independent | independent |
| Referenceable from outside | no | yes | yes |
| Reverse scan | contiguous prefix range | range scan if the key leads with the FK, else an index probe | as the dependent case, from the head side only |

**In the `Component` case the generated field stores no bytes.** It is a virtual column projecting the identifier prefix, typed `:> Document` — the same trick as `origin_server`, where "the projected bytes *are* the answer; a declared field would have been a stored copy of them, free to disagree" (`docs/transaction-graph.md:237-241`). At most one such field per child, since a component has exactly one parent.

This closes a real gap. Today a `Component`'s parent edge has **no name**, so `Request >< RequestHeader` fails the "no `:>` edge connects the two" check as written (`docs/schema/queries.md:127`) and there is no documented way to join a component to its parent. `:<` names the edge from both ends and makes the join legal in either direction, with the bytes unchanged.

**The trait changes the bytes, not the query** — the sentence `docs/schema/queries.md:234-240` already makes about nested tables, holding here unchanged.

### Two shard roots

A true many-to-many linking table is **not rejected and does not become its own root.** It is a dependent, and the head rule already decides it:

```
table app.commerce.Order : UserData {
  customer :> Customer,
  order_num : Int,
  unique orderRef { customer, order_num },

  tags :< OrderTag {
    tag :> Tag,
    unique orderTagRef { order, tag }     -- `order` first: this shard
  }
}
```

- `{ order, tag }` reaches two roots, so the **first FK determines placement** (`docs/schema/tables.md:176-177`; OQ-005, `docs/open-questions.md:373`). `OrderTag` lands in `Order`'s shard.
- The edge to `Tag` crosses a shard, which warns and names the edge (OQ-005, `docs/open-questions.md:362`).
- Writing `unique orderTagRef { tag, order }` instead places it in `Tag`'s shard while the source text reads as though `Order` owns it. Warn on that disagreement between nesting and key order.
- **Placement is in the key, never in the nesting.** That is what keeps the nested and flat forms interchangeable.
- It **may** carry `: Component` — a component references outward freely (`docs/schema/traits.md:222`) — buying the zero-byte link, the ordinal identity, and no key, at the cost of cascade with `Order` and of being unreferenceable from outside `Order`'s subtree. For a pure linking table that trade is usually right.

The honest cost, stated plainly: **reverse navigation from the non-head side is a scatter-gather across every shard of the head family.** `Tag.orders` cannot be a range scan. That is the row-rooted sharding model being visible in the declaration, not a defect of this construct — and the common case dissolves, because a tag-like table is normally `Reference`, and FKs to `Reference` do not participate in placement (`docs/schema/tables.md:167-168`), leaving one root and no cross-shard edge.

### The double-reference case

Two `:<` items may name the same child. At most one carries a body; the others name additional reverse edges and must give `via`.

```
table app.chat.User : UserData {
  username : Text unique,

  sent :< Message via sender {
    recipient :> User,                    -- the second reference, written by hand
    body       : Text,
    sent_at    : Timestamp,
    unique msgRef { sender, sent_at }
  },
  received :< Message via recipient       -- second reverse name, no body
}
```

`Message.recipient` is declared in the first body; `received` names it read backwards. Body items are a set, so resolution order does not matter.

### Trees

A `:<` naming its own table must be bodiless. It declares self-nesting, which for a `Component` is exactly the ordinal-path deepening `Doc` already uses:

```
table app.pm.Comment : Component {
  body    : Text,
  replies :< Comment
}
```

A stored `:>` to a component row is not representable — nothing specifies the on-disk form of a variable-length component identifier as a foreign value — so declaration nesting is the only spelling for a component tree, and this makes that explicit.

## Schema display

`:describe <name>` renders flat; `:describe <name> deep` renders nested.

`deep` is already reserved, on `verify shard QName deep` (`docs/schema/railroad.md:866`), and means the same thing here — recurse further. Zero new reserved words.

- **Flat** prints the containing table with bodiless `:<` items, then each child as its own `table` declaration. On a `Component` child the parent field prints in the virtual-columns section, not the field list.
- **`deep`** inlines the body of every child reachable by a named reverse edge, transitively, one level per `:<`. A cycle renders once and stops with a marker.
- Only **named** reverse edges nest. An unnamed inbound FK renders as a plain "referenced by" line. Otherwise `:describe User deep` inlines half the schema. Nesting is a claim of authorship and must be authored.

**Derivability holds, with one amendment.** The nested form is *almost* derivable from the flat FK graph — reading inbound `:>` edges backwards is mechanical. What is not derivable is the reverse relation's **name**, and that is real schema information because it is addressable in queries. Store it as an attribute of the FK field: `Comment.document` carries `reverse_name = comments`. The FK is the morphism, and the reverse name names the same morphism read backwards, so the name belongs on the edge.

With that, the graph stores **one canonical form** — the flat one — the nested form is a rendering, and the sugar is source-level only. Required property, and it is testable: **`:describe X deep` re-parses to the identical schema graph.**

## `Doc` stays distinct

`Doc indexed` does six things this construct does not (`docs/schema/documents.md:68-235`):

1. Generates **three** tables, not one: `…Node : Component`, `…Key : DocKeys` (`Reference, Extensible`, 2-byte interned tags), `…KeyRaw` carrying the owner's replication trait.
2. Gives the node's `key` a fallback chain `:> …Key | …KeyRaw | NoKey`.
3. Types `value` as a sum of every scalar plus `Object` and `Array`.
4. Discovers depth at ingest. The node's parent is another *node*, not the owning row, and nesting is by ordinal path — a shape no declaration states.
5. Runs the interning cap, spill, shape rules, demotion, and supersession, all `Configuration`-driven.
6. Keeps the **bytes authoritative** and makes shredding optional, because signature verification needs the exact bytes and unconditional shredding would make `Doc` unusable on the ingest path.

`:<` supplies only the first table, and only if you hand-write it.

**Do not redefine `Doc` in terms of `:<`.** The unification is at the rendering end, not the declaration end, and it is already half done — `docs/schema/documents.md:270-285` settled that the generated tables are named siblings precisely so anonymous sub-tables stay unnecessary. Take the other half: **`:describe app.log.Request deep` renders `RequestBodyNode` inline under the `body` field, as though it were a `:<` child.** Same renderer, distinct declaration.

`Doc` also gains something from this: the node table's parent edge becomes nameable, which it is not today.

## The name

Call it a **dependent declaration**, and the left-hand name a **reverse relation**. Not a "backreference".

For an FK `f : Comment → Document`, there is no arrow `Document → Comment` in the presented category. `Document.comments` is the **fibre** `f⁻¹(d)` — in Spivak's terms the object obtained by `Σ_f`, the left adjoint to the pullback `Δ_f`, not an inverse morphism. Three operational consequences fall straight out of that, and they are exactly the restrictions above:

- The fibre is **set-valued**, which is why the column is table-valued, why it cannot go in a key, and why it cannot appear in a `RecordLit`.
- It does not compose as a morphism does: `comments.author` is a *set* of authors, which is precisely what "a path through a table-valued column distributes" already says (`docs/schema/queries.md:266`).
- It adds **no morphism to the presentation**, so the four functor kinds are untouched. `:<` registers the same FK functor (kind 2) `:>` does; the reverse name is a projection, and "a `Behavior` is not a fifth kind — it enforces nothing, it projects" applies verbatim (`docs/category-model.md:128-130`).

Reverse traversal in an `assert` was already admissible — "every subsequent source must be reached by a `JoinClause` along a declared `:>` edge in either direction" (`docs/schema/railroad.md:252-254`) — so naming the fibre changes nothing about what an assert may say.

## Costs

| | Cost |
|---|---|
| Commit | Zero extra. The generated FK is checked like any FK. |
| Read | Zero unless requested — reverse columns are excluded from `*`. When requested: contiguous prefix scan (`Component`), range scan (key leads with the FK), else an index probe that automatic materialization proposes. |
| Bytes | Zero for `Component`; 12 for a dependent FK, identical to the flat spelling. The sugar costs nothing. |
| Cross-shard | Zero for components and same-shard dependents. For a two-root linking table, reverse traversal from the non-head side is a scatter-gather. |

**Advice worth putting in the docs:** declare the parent FK **first** in the child's candidate key. The rooted-key rule already pushes that way, and it makes reverse navigation a contiguous range scan at no extra cost.

## Access control

A reverse column returns child rows, and a child access assert runs per row on read. `docs/schema/constraints.md:232-243` already settles what happens: the row stays in the result with every field `Redacted`, including the key, because "the row's presence in the result is what tells a client 'you may not see this' as distinct from 'there is nothing here'." So `count comments` counts redacted rows. That is the existing, deliberate design — cardinality across an access boundary is visible by choice — and it needs no new rule. It does deserve one sentence in the docs, because a reverse count is the first place most authors will meet it.

### Grammar delta (per-item; see integrated version before applying)

All changes to `docs/schema/railroad.md`.

**1. Add `BackRefDecl` to `BodyItem` (Tables, bindings, traits):**

```ebnf
BodyItem     ::= FieldDecl
               | BackRefDecl
               | '*'
               | UniqueDecl
               | AssertDecl
               | EventDecl
               | HandlerDecl
               | OrderByDecl
               | FunctionDecl

BackRefDecl  ::= Ident ':<' QName SubTableTraits? ( 'via' Ident )? SubTableBody?
```

`RefToken`, `FieldDecl`, and `TraitItem` are **unchanged**. `BackRefDecl` is not a `TraitItem`: the generated FK must name a concrete table, and a trait is not one.

**2. Amend the maximal-munch table (Functions and Expressions → Lexing):**

| Prefix | Tokens |
|---|---|
| `:` | `:`, `:>`, `:<` |

No other row changes. Note beside it: `:` cannot begin an `Atom`, so no expression admits a token after `<` that starts with `:`; the `<` family is untouched and `<:` is deliberately not the spelling.

**3. Amend `MetaCommand` (REPL):**

```ebnf
MetaCommand  ::= ':use' QName
               | ':describe' QName 'deep'?
               | ':history' QName HistoryOpt*
               | ':commit'
               | ':rollback'
               | ':explain' Query
               | ':help'
```

**4. New "constraints not expressible in the grammar" bullets, under Tables, bindings, traits:**

- A `BackRefDecl` declares nothing on the containing table. It declares or amends the table its `QName` names, adding a `:>` field back; `via` names that field, defaulting to the containing table's name in `lower_snake_case`. Namespace defaults to the containing table's; a qualified `QName` places it elsewhere.
- At most one `BackRefDecl` naming a given child may carry a `SubTableBody`. Further ones name additional reverse edges and must carry `via`.
- A `SubTableBody` on a `BackRefDecl` is a redeclaration of the child and diffs under [evolution.md](evolution.md#redeclare-a-table). Declaring one table twice in a single commit is an error.
- The generated `:>` field's origin address is the `BackRefDecl`'s path, so redeclaring the child cannot drop it. It is dropped by `deprecate` on the `BackRefDecl`.
- A `BackRefDecl` that adds a `:>` to a populated child is refused unless the type carries a `Null`-derived variant; the diagnostic names it.
- Where the child carries `Component`, the generated field is a **virtual column** projecting the identifier prefix and stores no bytes. At most one such field per child.
- A `BackRefDecl` whose `QName` names the containing table must be bodiless.
- A `BackRefDecl`'s `Ident` names a table-valued virtual column on the containing table. It is excluded from `'*'` and rejected in a `UniqueDecl`, a `DefaultClause`, a `RecordLit`, an `OrderByDecl`, and with `'unique'` or `IndexedClause`.
- `: TraitList` on a projected reverse column is rejected — the child's replication trait is declared, not projected.
- `JoinClause`'s `as` is optional where the query names the reverse edge, since that edge supplies the column name.

**5. Reserved Words: no additions.** Add to the "words considered and not reserved" prose:

- **`has`**, **`owns`**, **`from`**, and **`by`**, as a keyword for the dependent declaration. `has` and `owns` are plausible field names, which is the ground on which `write` and `open` were refused; `from` was withdrawn with `SourceClause` and resurrecting it in a new meaning is worse than a symbol; `by` already carries two meanings (`order by`, `by GrainRef`).
- **`nested`** and **`flat`**, as `:describe` modifiers. `deep` is already reserved by `verify shard … deep` and means recurse further, which is what nesting is.

`via` gains a position (naming the child's FK back, the same job it does in a `NameClause`) and `deep` gains a position (`:describe`). Neither is new.

### Interactions

- Four functor kinds — untouched. `:<` registers the same foreign-key functor (kind 2) that `:>` does; the reverse name is a projection, and `docs/category-model.md:128-130`'s argument that a `Behavior` is not a fifth kind applies verbatim.
- Candidate keys and sharding — the child declares its key in its own body, so nesting is presentational and placement stays in the key (`docs/schema/tables.md:156-190`). A `Component` child is key-exempt. A two-root linking table is placed by the first FK in its key (head rule, `docs/schema/tables.md:176-177`); nesting under the other end without reordering the key is a warning.
- Component ordinals and the zero-byte parent link — unchanged in bytes. The generated field on a `Component` child is a virtual column projecting the identifier prefix, the same construction as `origin_server` (`docs/transaction-graph.md:237-241`). This also closes a live gap: today a component's parent edge has no name, so `Request >< RequestHeader` fails the no-`:>`-edge check at `docs/schema/queries.md:127`.
- Derived-key meaningful/degenerate — a reverse column in a projection preserves the parent's key, so a binding like `Document { title, count comments as n }` stays meaningful and incrementally refreshable. Maintenance runs on child writes: free when the child is in the parent's shard, cross-shard for a two-root linking table.
- Writability — a `RecordLit` naming a reverse column is a compile-time error. The insert-decomposition rule is one mutation per base table (OQ-005, `docs/open-questions.md:390`) and a reverse column is many rows, so the arity is wrong. A multi-row nested insert would need a list literal, which the expression grammar does not have; none is proposed.
- Effect ladder — untouched. No new evaluation position, nothing that could read the clock, no new lift.
- Append-only and the version chain — untouched. The child is an ordinary table with an ordinary version chain; the nested source form is not stored.
- `Doc` shredding — unchanged in declaration, gains the nested rendering and a nameable parent edge. `Doc` is not redefined in terms of `:<`.
- Access asserts on read — a child access assert runs per row of a reverse column, and `docs/schema/constraints.md:232-243` already settles the outcome: the row is present with every field `Redacted`, so `count comments` counts redacted rows. Deliberate existing behaviour; one sentence in the docs because a reverse count is where authors first meet it.
- Functor transparency — the reverse name resolves at plan time to the existing FK edge traversed backwards, so no new DSL term is introduced and the optimizer, static access analysis, and coercion-path derivation see exactly what they see today.
- Replication traits — `SubTableTraits` sets the child's trait as it does on an inline sub-table. This exposes a pre-existing gap rather than creating one: nothing currently forbids a `Reference` child with a `:>` into shard-local `UserData`. Flagged, not legislated here.
- Materialization — reverse navigation on a non-`Component` child is an ordinary candidate arrangement for the automatic proposer (OQ-005, `docs/open-questions.md:388`). No `create index` is implied.
- `deprecate` and `prune` — `deprecate <Parent>.<reverse-name>` retires the relation and its generated FK; `deprecate <Child>.<fk>` retires the edge and the reverse name with it. Cascade on parent deprecation follows `Component` edges only, unchanged (`docs/schema/tables.md:461-464`).

### Alternatives rejected

- `<:` as asked — the standard subtyping operator in type theory, Scala, F<:, Julia, Ceylon, and PVS, meaning the reverse of what is intended, in a language where `:` already means subtype (`type Email : Text`). It also joins the `<`/`<=` family, which is live in expression position, where `:` and `:>` are not. The purely lexical objection is weak (`:` cannot start an `Atom`, so `a < :b` is not a program) and should not be overstated; the semantic collision is what kills it.
- `<\` — genuinely ambiguous, not merely ugly. `Atom` includes `Lambda` (`docs/schema/railroad.md:487`), so `x < \y -> y` is grammatical today; `<\` would collide with `< \` under maximal munch. Decisive.
- A keyword — `has`, `owns`, `from`, or `by`. `has` and `owns` are plausible field names, the exact ground on which `write` and `open` were refused (`docs/schema/railroad.md:938-943`). `from` was withdrawn with `SourceClause` (`docs/schema/railroad.md:145-147`) and resurrecting it in a new meaning is worse than adding a symbol. `by` already carries `order by` and `by GrainRef`. Every one of these costs a reserved word; `:<` costs none.
- Reusing `:>` with the direction implied by position — the parser cannot do it. Capitalization is style and not grammar (`docs/schema/railroad.md:41-46`), so `Comment :> Document` inside `Document`'s body is indistinguishable from a field named `Comment` referencing `Document`. It would also make one token mean two opposite relations.
- An inline sub-table body on a field that is not a column — that is what this proposal is, minus the operator; without a distinguishing token it collapses into the previous item and is unparseable for the same reason.
- `:<` with no left-hand name — the parser needs a distinguishing left-hand token, and discarding the name throws away the only genuinely new capability: an addressable reverse relation that closes the mandatory-`as` case and gives `Component` parents a join edge they currently lack.
- Defaulting the child to `Component` — it would make cascade delete the default for a construct authors will reach for constantly, against the 'nothing is destroyed' invariant, and would silently forbid outside references to the child (`docs/schema/traits.md:221`). Declared, as on a forward inline sub-table.
- Letting the nesting decide placement — it would make the flat and nested renderings inequivalent, destroying exactly the property that lets `:describe … deep` be a rendering rather than a second source of truth.
- Nesting every inbound FK under `deep` — `:describe User deep` would inline half the schema. Only named reverse edges nest; nesting is a claim of authorship and must be authored.
- New reserved words `nested` and `flat` for `:describe` — `deep` is already reserved (`verify shard … deep`) and already means recurse further.
- Redefining `Doc` in terms of `:<` — it would have to express three generated tables, a fallback key chain, an ADT value union, ingest-discovered depth, and Configuration-driven interning with a cap and spill, none of which a declaration states. The unification worth taking is the shared renderer, not a shared declaration.
- Storing the reverse name as a node on the parent — it belongs on the FK field, because the FK is the morphism and the reverse name names that same morphism read backwards. Putting it on the parent would create a second graph object for one fact.

### OQ impact

- Amends OQ-005 (Schema DSL Syntax, ✓ ANSWERED) in place with one bullet: `name :< Child : Trait via fk { … }` declares a dependent table inline with the foreign key on the child, closing the 1:many gap that `address :> Address { … }` cannot express and that `docs/schema/tables.md:421-429`'s own `headers` example silently mis-states. `:<` rather than `<:` because `<:` is the standard subtyping operator and `:` already means subtype here, and because `:` and `:>` are absent from expression position while `<` and `<=` are not; the token pairs with `:>` the way `Data.Sequence`'s `ViewL`/`ViewR` do. The production is `NameClause`'s shape with `:<` for `as`, so no reserved word is added and `via`/`deep` gain positions only. The left-hand name is an addressable table-valued reverse relation, excluded from `*` and rejected in keys and record literals, which makes it a navigation feature rather than sugar and closes the mandatory-`as` case at `docs/schema/queries.md:134-146`. Placement stays in the child's declared key, so nesting is presentational and the graph stores one flat canonical form plus a `reverse_name` attribute on the FK edge; `:describe … deep` renders the nested form and round-trips. Rejected: `<:`, `<\` (ambiguous with `< \`, since `Atom` includes `Lambda`), `has`/`owns`/`from`/`by`, and direction-by-position (capitalization is style, not grammar). Categorically the name denotes a fibre `f⁻¹(d)` / `Σ_f`, not an inverse morphism, which is why it is set-valued and why it adds no functor kind.
- No new OQ number. Every sub-decision here is settled by rules already in the docs — the head rule for two roots, `Component` invariants for ownership, redeclaration and origin addressing for amendment, and the `Redacted` rule for reverse counts across an access boundary. Recording it as an open question would bloat the file.
- Two adjacent gaps worth flagging in the relevant files rather than as OQs: (a) `docs/schema/evolution.md:274` promises `NotFound` for an added field, which a bare `:>` cannot hold — this proposal refuses the case rather than widening it; (b) nothing currently forbids a `Reference` table holding a `:>` into shard-local `UserData`, which `SubTableTraits` on a `BackRefDecl` makes easy to write by accident.

### Implementation notes

**Lexer.** One token. Extend the `:` munch state to accept `<` as well as `>`. The `<` state is untouched.

**Parser.** One new `BodyItem` alternative. `BackRefDecl` is `NameClause`'s shape with a different lead token and an optional trailing body, so the trait-then-`via` sub-parsers are already written. Keeping it a separate `BodyItem` rather than a `RefToken` alternative on `FieldDecl` is what avoids rejecting five inapplicable clauses (`unique`, `indexed`, `= default`, `where`) by constraint, and it makes the diagnostics say what is wrong.

**Desugarer.** Runs before name resolution and produces the flat form: emit or amend the child `TableDecl`, insert the generated `:>` field with `origin = <parent>.<reverse-name>`, and attach `reverse_name` to that field's schema node. Everything downstream sees a schema with no `:<` in it. This is where the round-trip property is won or lost — the desugarer must be the only consumer of the construct.

**GADT DSL.** No new term. The generated FK is the existing kind-2 functor. A reverse column in a projection compiles to the same table-valued-column term `group` already produces for `rows`, so `count`/`sum`/path distribution work with no change to the expression evaluator, and the optimizer, static access analysis, coercion-path derivation, and the IDE keep seeing the structure they see today.

**Storage.** Nothing new. `Component` child: the existing ordinal prefix; the named parent field is a projection computed at read, alongside `created_at`, `origin_server`, and `ordinal`. Dependent child: an ordinary 12-byte FK, byte-identical to the flat spelling.

**Planner.** Three cases for a reverse traversal, chosen off the declaration:
- `Component` — contiguous LMDB prefix range scan over the parent's byte prefix. Free.
- Dependent whose candidate key leads with the parent FK — range scan on the base arrangement. Free.
- Anything else — index probe on the child's FK; the automatic materialization proposer picks it up from `system.telemetry` after the first slow run.
- Non-head side of a two-root linking table — scatter-gather across every shard of the head family. Emit the cost in `:explain` and warn at schema commit.

**Commit checks.** Two declarations of one table in a commit; at most one body per child; `via` required on the second and later `:<` naming one child; self-`:<` must be bodiless; a `:<` adding a `:>` to a populated child without an absence variant; the disagreement between nesting and key order for a two-root child. All are schema-graph checks with no data access except the populated-child count, which the blast-radius machinery in `docs/integrity.md` already computes.

**CLI.** `:describe … deep` is a renderer over the flat graph: walk inbound `:>` edges carrying a `reverse_name`, inline the child body, mark cycles. Add a round-trip test — parse, desugar, render `deep`, re-parse, compare graphs — because that test is the whole justification for calling the construct sugar.

### References

- David Spivak, *Functorial Data Migration* — a schema is a finitely presented category and an FK is a morphism; `Δ_f`, `Σ_f`, `Π_f` are the three migration functors. The reverse of an FK is not an arrow in the presentation: `Document.comments` is the fibre `f⁻¹(d)`, i.e. `Σ_f` viewed over `Document`. This is why the column is set-valued, why it cannot enter a key or a record literal, and why the construct adds no functor kind. It is also why 'backreference' is a misleading name — there is no reverse arrow to name.
- Rails `has_many` / `inverse_of` — the reverse name is association metadata, never a column, and Rails cannot infer it reliably when several FKs target one model, which is why `inverse_of` exists. Direct evidence that the reverse name must be authored and that the multi-FK case needs an explicit edge selector (`via` here).
- Django `related_name` — defaults the reverse accessor to `<model>_set` and requires `related_name` the moment two FKs target one model, or it raises a system-check error. The default-plus-override shape recommended here, and a warning against defaulting the name too cleverly.
- Ecto `has_many :comments, foreign_key: :document_id` — the closest analogue. The parent schema declares the association, the FK lives once on the child, and the association is not loaded unless `preload`ed. That last property is exactly the `*`-exclusion rule: an unbounded reverse set must never ride along on a wildcard read.
- Prisma relation fields with `@relation("name")` — both ends are written and the relation name disambiguates multiple FKs between one pair of models; Prisma raises a validation error on an ambiguous relation. Same check as 'at most one `:<` per child may carry a body, later ones must give `via`'.
- GraphQL connection pattern — reverse edges as first-class fields, with pagination mandated precisely because reverse cardinality is unbounded. Corroborates excluding the reverse column from `*` and admitting aggregates over it rather than implicit materialization.
- Haskell `Data.Sequence` — `ViewL` uses `:<` and `ViewR` uses `:>`, as left-view and right-view. DataCode already took `:>`; `:<` is its established partner. Haskell's rule that an operator beginning with `:` is a data constructor makes both read as constructors, which is what they are.
- Scala, Julia, Ceylon, PVS, and Cardelli's F<: — `<:` is subtype-of throughout. A type-literate reader will read `comments <: Comment` as a subtyping claim, which is both wrong and, in a language where `:` already means subtype, redundant.
- SQL — has no reverse relation at all; the reverse of an FK is spelled as a correlated subquery or a join every time. The absence is what makes `has_many` the first thing every ORM adds, and it is the gap this construct closes at the schema level rather than per query.
- TutorialD / the relational model — a relvar has no notion of a reverse relation either; navigation is by explicit join. `docs/schema/README.md:31` places DataCode closer to TutorialD than SQL, so naming the fibre is a genuine addition to that lineage and should be justified as one, not assumed.

### Adversarial critique

**Fatal objections**

- THE MOTIVATING GAP IS CONTRADICTED BY THE DOCS, AND THE PROPOSAL PICKS A SIDE SILENTLY. The proposal's headline evidence is that `headers :> RequestHeader : Component { name, value }` (tables.md:421-429) 'reads as many headers and means one', calling it 'the doc tripping over this' and instructing a doc_edit to REWRITE it as `:<`. But queries.md:234-236 says the opposite in the same breath the proposal cites elsewhere: 'A `Component` nested table is a **column**, addressed as a path (`Agg.LinkedTable`), identified by `Ordinal`, and destroyed with its parent — **the same construct as an inline component sub-table** ([tables.md](tables.md#component-sub-tables))'. That link points at the `headers` section. `rows` renamed `as Sale : Component` holds MANY rows; queries.md says `headers` is the same construct. Three further facts favour table-valued: `Ordinal` exists at all and is 'how document order is stated in a query' (tables.md:45-46, transaction-graph.md:622-640) — ordinals are meaningless for a 1:1 field; traits.md:224 caps components at '2^32 per parent', per PARENT not per field; traits.md:226 writes 'a **1:1** component such as an address', which only needs qualifying if 1:many components exist. Meanwhile tables.md:326 says `:>` wraps 'the referenced table's `DataId`' and a Component row HAS no `DataId` (traits.md:199), so the singular reading is not even well-typed. So the docs genuinely disagree with each other, and the proposal asserts one resolution as settled fact to manufacture its gap. Consequence: if the table-valued reading is right — and the weight of evidence says it is — then 1:many inline is ALREADY WRITABLE for owned children and `:<` is a second spelling for it. The doc_edit instruction ('FIX the example at lines 421-429') would delete the only illustration of the 1:many component form and legislate an open question inside a change advertised as additive sugar.

- THE LANGUAGE ALREADY ANSWERS 'THE LINKING TABLE NEEDS A SECOND STATEMENT', AND THE PROPOSAL NEVER MENTIONS IT. auth.md:476-500 plus queries.md:527-557 is DataCode's settled idiom for exactly the user's grievance: declare the linking table once, then bind a derived table over it — `system.auth.ServiceAccount = User >< AccountKind { User.*, AccountKind.purpose } where kind is Service` — and auth.md:499 states the payoff verbatim: '**The call site never names the linking table.**' It is strictly stronger than `:<` on the axis that matters most: the binding is WRITABLE (queries.md:543-549 — meaningful derived key, `:>` joins, required fields fixed by the `where`), so an insert decomposes into both base tables with the linking row created implicitly (auth.md:496-499). The proposal, by contrast, makes `RecordLit` naming a reverse column a compile-time error and offers no write path at all. Its `references` section cites Rails, Django, Ecto, Prisma, GraphQL, SQL and TutorialD and omits the mechanism already in this repo that covers the same user complaint. Per the brief, 'this needs no new syntax, here is the existing way' is the strongest critique available, and for the user's stated grievance the existing way is a `Binding`.

- THE TWO-SHARD-ROOT ARGUMENT RESTS ON A CITATION THAT DOES NOT EXIST AND MISSES THE RULE THAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS IT. The proposal states twice — in pushback #3 and again in the two-roots section — that 'an outbound FK crossing a shard is a warning naming the edge, not an error (OQ-005, `docs/open-questions.md:362`)'. Line 362 of open-questions.md is '**Asserts are anchored.**' — about `self`-rooting, nothing to do with cross-shard FKs. The warning rule is real but lives at constraints.md:187-189, and it is scoped to the read cost of an ASSERT's remote hop, not to a stored FK on a linking table. What actually governs a two-root linking table is open-questions.md:144, which the proposal never cites: '**A constraint whose revalidation set crosses shards cannot be `enforce always`** ... such an attachment is restricted to `enforce forward`, `monitor`, or `repair into`, and the breach surfaces as a `system.integrity.Violation` instead of a rejected write.' Referential integrity on `OrderTag.tag :> Tag` where `Tag` is a different shard root is exactly a revalidation set crossing shards. So the proposal's cheerful 'A true many-to-many linking table is **not rejected** ... the head rule already decides it' omits the actual price: the second FK is **not enforce-always**, and the many-to-many is only eventually referentially consistent. That is the whole reason linking tables are awkward, which the brief demanded be answered head-on, and it is the one consequence the answer leaves out.

- `deprecate <Parent>.<reverse-name>` IS INCOHERENT FOR A `Component` CHILD. The proposal's interactions state uniformly: '`deprecate <Parent>.<reverse-name>` retires the relation **and its generated FK**'. For a `Component` child the generated field is — by the proposal's own design — a virtual projection of the identifier prefix, and traits.md:220 is categorical: 'A component cannot be reparented | **The parent is the identifier**; moving it would change its identity.' There is no FK to retire; retiring it would purport to remove the child's identity. Worse, it collides with 'nothing is destroyed': the surviving component rows would be addressable by nothing. The rule has to bifurcate — on a `Component` child `deprecate` of the reverse name drops the NAME only, never the edge, and the child is retired only as a whole table — and the proposal states it as one rule in both the recommendation and the grammar_delta bullet ('It is dropped by `deprecate` on the `BackRefDecl`').

**Corrections**

- THE HASKELL-READER DEFENCE IS BACKWARDS, AND CLAUDE.md MAKES THAT THE TIE-BREAKER. The proposal argues '`Data.Sequence` pairs `:<` (`ViewL`) with `:>` (`ViewR`) as left-view and right-view. DataCode already took `:>`; `:<` is its partner.' In `Data.Sequence`, `data ViewL a = EmptyL | a :< Seq a` — the SINGLE element is on the left and the SEQUENCE on the right. Read against `comments :< Comment`, that says `comments` is one element and `Comment` is the collection: precisely inverted from the intent. And `ViewR` is `Seq a :> a` — many on the left — whereas DataCode's `:>` is `field :> Table`, one on the left. DataCode's `:>` is already not `Data.Sequence`'s `:>`, so invoking the pair is post-hoc and cuts the wrong way if a reader takes it seriously. Drop the argument. What survives, and is sufficient: an operator beginning with `:` is a CONSTRUCTOR in Haskell, and DataCode has already made the `:` family the structural-declaration family (`:` subtypes, `:>` references), so `:<` reads as a third constructor in a family a reader has already learned. Keep `:<`; delete the `ViewL`/`ViewR` sentence. (The `<:` objection itself is correct and is in fact stronger than stated: OQ-005 at open-questions.md:391 records that 'a table is a type — `table T : Trait` uses the same `:` that `type A : B` does', so `comments <: Comment` is a WELL-FORMED sentence in DataCode's own subtyping discipline that happens to be false — the worst kind of collision, a plausible misreading rather than a parse error.)

- THE TRAIT DEFAULT CONTRADICTS `group`'s WHILE CLAIMING READER TRANSFER FROM IT. The proposal writes 'A reader who knows `rows as Sale : UserData via product` already knows this construct' and then inverts that construct's default: queries.md:230-232 says 'Defaults: the nested table carries **`Component`**, and its FK is named after the group row's table in `lower_snake_case`', which is also recorded in OQ-005 at open-questions.md:383. The proposal makes `:<` default to the parent's replication trait instead. Same clause shape, same position, opposite default — a reader who transfers from `group` gets it exactly wrong, and silently, because both parse. Pick one: either default `:<` to `Component` (consistent, and the cascade objection is answered by the fact that `group`'s nested table already cascades), or keep the dependent default and DELETE the reader-transfer claim, adding a sentence to queries.md and tables.md noting the deliberate asymmetry and why. The proposal's stated reason — '`group`'s nested table defaults to `Component` because its rows are already inside the group row; here they are not' — is a restatement of the choice, not a reason.

- `SubTableTraits` ON A BODILESS `:<` IS AMBIGUOUS AND SHOULD JUST BE FORBIDDEN. `SubTableTraits ::= ':' TraitList`, `TraitList ::= QName (',' QName)*`, and body items are `,`-separated (railroad.md:51-54, 200-203). With no `SubTableBody` to terminate it, `comments :< Comment : Component, owner :> User` has `TraitList` munch `owner` as a second trait before failing on `:>`. This latent hazard already exists in `NameClause` (railroad.md:630) but is rare there; the proposal makes it the COMMON case, because the bodiless `:<` is precisely the flat canonical form the graph stores and `:describe` prints. Fix, and it is principled rather than a parser patch: forbid `SubTableTraits` on a `BackRefDecl` that carries no `SubTableBody`. A bodiless `:<` names an existing child declared elsewhere and has no business setting that child's replication trait. This also closes, for free, the '`Reference` child with a `:>` into shard-local `UserData`' accident the proposal itself flags in oq_impact (c) and questions_for_user #6 — that accident is only reachable through `SubTableTraits`.

- `count <reverse>` IN A `where` IS AN ORACLE, AND THE PROPOSAL DECLARES IT SETTLED WHEN IT IS NOT. The proposal cites constraints.md:232-243 and concludes 'That is the existing, deliberate design — cardinality across an access boundary is visible by choice — and it needs no new rule.' Read what constraints.md:240-243 actually justifies: keys survive as `Redacted` in a RESULT SET the requester already reached, and the rationale is 'the case that matters is a scan, where surviving keys would enumerate the identities of rows the requester may not read.' A count is not a field, so no assert redacts it: `count comments` returns the TRUE cardinality of rows whose every field is `Redacted`. The proposal's own example `Document where count comments == 0` then promotes that leak from a visible artefact of a returned row into a FILTER PREDICATE — `Document where count comments > 5` enumerates parents by hidden-child cardinality at scan scale with no child row ever appearing. The capability pre-exists via `>< ... group`, so this is not a new hole, but the proposal makes it one token and then waves it through. Either state a rule (an aggregate over a reverse relation whose child carries an access assert is evaluated post-redaction, or is rejected in a `where`), or say plainly that it is a known leak and record it — do not call it settled.

- THE `Component` VIRTUAL PARENT COLUMN COLLIDES WITH THE PROPOSAL'S OWN TREE RULE. The recommendation adds a virtual column on a `Component` child 'typed `:> Document`', modelled on `origin_server` (transaction-graph.md:237-241 — correct citation, and a good precedent, since transaction-graph.md:570-576 already types a virtual column `:> system.shards.Node` and tables.md:213-218 makes such columns key-eligible). But nesting appends an ordinal per level (transaction-graph.md:493), so a level-2 component's parent is a level-1 COMPONENT row, and the proposal's own Trees section states 'A stored `:>` to a component row is not representable — nothing specifies the on-disk form of a variable-length component identifier as a foreign value.' The virtual column on a nested component is therefore typed `:>` a component table, which the same document forbids. It is resolvable (nothing is stored; the projection is the prefix), but the proposal states both rules without noticing they touch, and transaction-graph.md's virtual-column table would need the row spelled carefully.

- THE `via` DEFAULT IS UNDER-SPECIFIED AND FRAGILE. 'defaults to this table's name in `lower_snake_case`' uses the UNQUALIFIED name, so `app.pm.Document` and `app.crm.Document` both nesting `Comment` generate two fields named `document` on one child — a collision the 'at most one body per child, later ones must give `via`' rule does not catch, because it is scoped to one parent's body. Separately, the proposal's own `OrderTag` example writes `unique orderTagRef { order, tag }` inside a child body naming `order`, a field the DESUGARER inserts. That works, but renaming the parent table silently changes the generated field name and breaks every child body that referenced it, with the error surfacing in the child rather than at the rename. Require `via` whenever the child body mentions the generated field, or drop the default entirely — one word bought at the price of a rename hazard is a poor trade in a language whose whole evolution story is that renames are projections you can see.

- THE MAXIMAL-MUNCH `:` ROW IS ALREADY INCOMPLETE AND THE AMENDMENT PROPAGATES THAT. railroad.md:583-589 lists the `:` prefix as yielding `:`, `:>`. But railroad.md:766-772 defines `':use'`, `':describe'`, `':history'`, `':commit'`, `':rollback'`, `':explain'`, `':help'` as literal tokens — seven more members of the `:` family the table does not list. Adding `:<` to a row that already misstates its own family in the file that calls itself 'the single source of truth for DataCode syntax' is a defect worth fixing in the same edit: either list the meta-commands, or respell `MetaCommand` as `':' 'describe'` etc. and say the family is `:`, `:>`, `:<` only. (The substantive lexical finding is correct and correctly hedged: `:` cannot start an `Atom` (railroad.md:482-490), so `a < :b` is not a program and BOTH `<:` and `:<` lex unambiguously. No currently-valid program places `<` immediately after `:` — every `:` in the grammar is followed by a `QName`, `TypeExpr`, or `TypeSig`, all of which begin with an identifier or `(`. The semantic collision is the whole case against `<:`, exactly as the proposal says.)

- CITATION AUDIT — one materially wrong, three off by one or two, the rest correct. WRONG: `docs/open-questions.md:362` for the cross-shard-FK-is-a-warning rule (cited TWICE, load-bearing for pushback #3 and the two-roots section) — line 362 is 'Asserts are anchored'; the rule is at `docs/schema/constraints.md:187-189`. OFF: `railroad.md:487` for '`Atom` includes `Lambda`' — `Lambda` is line 485, 487 is `LetExpr` (claim true, cite off by two, and the `<\` rejection it supports stands); `tables.md:176-177` for the head rule — it is 175-176; `railroad.md:145-147` for `SourceClause` withdrawn — it is 146-149. VERIFIED CORRECT: railroad.md:41-46 (capitalization is style), :630 (`NameClause`), :482-490 (`Atom`), :866 (`verify shard ... deep`), :938-943 (`write`/`open` not reserved), :160-162 (`SubTableBody` only with `:>`); tables.md:167-168, :205-212, :373-409, :391-409, :421-429, :461-464; queries.md:127, :134-146, :215-249, :234-240, :266-273; documents.md:34-38, :115-118, :99-106, :41-51, :270-285; evolution.md:10-25, :15-16, :98-99, :274; constraints.md:232-243; traits.md:221, :222; category-model.md:128-130; transaction-graph.md:237-241; open-questions.md:373, :388, :390, :391.

- WHAT SURVIVES INTACT AND SHOULD BE KEPT. (1) `:<` over `<:` — right call, right reasons, and the pushback's terminology correction is right: there is no 'Doc trait'; `Doc` is a type (documents.md:35-38), `indexed` is the storage hint, `DocKeys` is the trait (documents.md:115-118). (2) Storing `reverse_name` as an attribute of the FK FIELD rather than on the parent — this is the load-bearing insight, and it is what makes derivability hold. CONFIRMED, not refuted: with the name on the edge, the flat form is the single canonical graph form, the nested form is a pure rendering, and `:describe X deep` round-trips. The proposal is right that this is the property that decides whether the construct is sugar, and right to demand a round-trip test as its proof. (3) The categorical framing is correct and is the best thing in the document: for `f : Comment → Document` there is no arrow `Document → Comment`, so `Document.comments` is the fibre `f^-1(d)`, not a dual morphism, which is WHY it is set-valued, why it cannot enter a key or a `RecordLit`, and why the four functor kinds are untouched — the same argument category-model.md:128-130 makes for `Behavior`. 'Dependent declaration' / 'reverse relation' over 'backreference' is the right name. (4) `deep` reuse costs no reserved word (railroad.md:866, 881). (5) Excluding the reverse column from `*`, and the Ecto-`preload` precedent for it, is correct. (6) Naming the reverse edge does make `as` optional at queries.md:134-146 — but see missed_interactions on the narrower `Request >< RequestHeader` claim.

**Missed interactions**

- open-questions.md:144 — a constraint whose revalidation set crosses shards CANNOT be `enforce always` and is coerced to `forward`/`monitor`/`repair into`, with the breach surfacing as a `system.integrity.Violation`. The second FK of any true many-to-many linking table is exactly this. So the proposal's two-roots answer needs one more line: the cross-root edge is not enforce-always, and schema commit reports the coercion (open-questions.md:144 already requires that report, 'because an `enforce always` that silently became `forward` is the read-behaviour-changed-without-touching-a-field case this file already requires be surfaced').

- traits.md:221 — 'Nothing outside the parent's subtree may reference a component' — makes the proposal's advice 'It **may** carry `: Component` ... For a pure linking table that trade is usually right' actively dangerous for the Enrollment-shaped case. Order/Tag/OrderTag is fine because an order-tag has no meaning apart from the order. Student/Course/Enrollment is not: an enrollment carries a grade, is referenced by transcripts, and outlives neither party trivially. Making it a `Component` of `Student` means deleting the student destroys the enrollment record in the same transaction (tables.md:461-464) and nothing may ever reference it. The proposal offers one blanket recommendation for two shapes that differ on exactly the invariant `Component` encodes. Say which is which, or drop the recommendation.

- MATERIALIZATION AMPLIFICATION WHEN THE HEAD IS `Reference`. The proposal's best save on two roots is that 'a tag-like table is normally `Reference`, and FKs to `Reference` do not participate in placement (tables.md:167-168), leaving one root and no cross-shard edge'. True for placement — but its interactions bullet then claims `Document { title, count comments as n }` is 'incrementally refreshable ... free when the child is in the parent's shard, cross-shard for a two-root linking table'. Run that on `Tag { name, count orders }`: `Tag` is `Reference`, so it replicates to EVERY server (documents.md:120-125, traits.md), so maintaining that count means every `OrderTag` insert in any shard touches a cluster-wide replicated row. That is not 'cross-shard', it is cluster-wide write amplification on a per-order operation, and it is the one case the `Reference` save creates rather than dissolves.

- THE `Doc` CASE — THE USER'S ACTUAL MOTIVATING EXAMPLE — SUPPLIES ZERO EVIDENCE FOR THE GAP, AND NEITHER THE REQUEST NOR THE PROPOSAL SAYS SO. The user's premise is 'the Doc table type is a linking table ... a lot of the benefit of defining subtables inside another table's definition is broken when you have to make another statement to define the linking table'. But `Doc indexed` GENERATES its three tables (documents.md:68-90) — there is no second statement to write, the node table's parent link is the identifier prefix with no FK at all (documents.md:100-105), and documents.md:270-285 already settled that they are named siblings precisely so anonymous nesting stays unnecessary. The proposal corrects the 'Doc trait' terminology and correctly refuses to redefine `Doc` in terms of `:<` (all six reasons hold), but never makes the decisive point: the one case the user pointed at costs zero extra statements, so it is not evidence of the burden the construct is meant to relieve.

- `Request >< RequestHeader` DOES NOT FAIL TODAY, SO ONE OF THE PROPOSAL'S TWO 'CLOSES A LIVE GAP' CLAIMS IS FALSE. The proposal asserts: 'today a `Component`'s parent edge has **no name**, so `Request >< RequestHeader` fails the "no `:>` edge connects the two" check as written (queries.md:127)'. But `headers :> RequestHeader : Component { ... }` (tables.md:424) IS a declared `:>` field — under either reading of what it denotes — so the edge exists and the join is legal. The claim is true only for `Doc`-generated node tables, where the owning field is `body : Doc` (`:`, not `:>`) and documents.md:71 declares `RequestBodyNode` with no reciprocal field anywhere. The proposal took a real gap in one generated case and generalized it to all components. Narrow the claim to `Doc` node tables — where, notably, `:<` cannot help either, because those tables are generated rather than declared.

- HISTORICAL `at` READS AND THE VERSIONED REVERSE NAME. Not addressed anywhere in the proposal. Because `reverse_name` is stored on the FK field's schema node, it is versioned like any field attribute — which is the right answer and makes `Document { count comments } at "..."` well defined. But the FK `Comment.document` may predate the reverse name, so the identical query resolves at head and fails at an earlier `at` moment with 'no such column'. That is consistent with how any renamed field behaves (evolution.md:55-66), and evolution.md:269-277's coercion path covers it, but it is the first construct where a NAME rather than a value is schema-node-dependent in a projection, and the docs should say so once.

- `AssertBody` ANCHORING ALREADY PERMITS REVERSE TRAVERSAL, WHICH THE PROPOSAL NOTES, BUT THE INTERACTION WITH ACCESS-ASSERT READ COST IS NOT COSTED. constraints.md:177-183 permits '`:>` edge in either direction' and bounds work to the row's connected component. A named reverse relation makes the reverse direction one token, which will get it written into access asserts far more often — and constraints.md:180-181 is explicit that 'an access assert runs on every read'. A reverse fibre is unbounded where a forward `:>` is exactly one row, so `assert x { self.comments ... }` is an unbounded read on every read of the parent, inside the one construct the anchoring rule exists to bound. The proposal's questions_for_user #4 gestures at this but frames it as a spelling question ('one presence spelling'); it is a cost question. Recommend rejecting the path form for the reason given, not the aesthetic one.

**Simpler alternative**

TWO CHANGES, NO NEW PRODUCTION, ONE RESERVED WORD — and they split the problem along the line the language already draws.

**(A) Say what a `:>` to a `Component` sub-table denotes. Zero grammar delta.** One paragraph in tables.md, under Component Sub-Tables: a `:>` field whose sub-table carries `Component` is **table-valued** — it holds that parent's component rows in `ordinal` order — exactly as `rows` is, which is what queries.md:234-236 already says when it calls the two 'the same construct'. Consequences fall out with no new syntax: `count headers`, `headers.name`, `max headers.ordinal` are the existing distribution rule (queries.md:266-273); `Request >< RequestHeader` is legal in both directions because the `:>` field is the edge; the field name is the accessor, which retires queries.md:235's competing `Agg.LinkedTable` path spelling. Add the reverse column to Ineligible Key Fields (tables.md:205-212) for the same unboundedness reason as `Doc`, and exclude it from `*`.

That resolves the `headers`-is-plural contradiction the proposal wanted to 'fix' by rewriting the example, and it delivers the user's actual request — inline 1:many sub-table declaration — for every child that is genuinely owned. Cost: one paragraph. No token, no `BodyItem`, no desugarer, no amendment semantics, no same-commit conflict rule, no populated-child refusal rule, no round-trip test.

**(B) If you still want a named reverse relation on a NON-owned child, put the name where the proposal already proved it has to be stored: on the child's FK.**

```ebnf
FieldDecl ::= Ident RefToken TypeExpr SubTableTraits? SubTableBody?
              ( 'reverse' Ident )?
              'unique'? IndexedClause? DefaultClause? WhereClause?
```

```
table app.pm.Comment : UserData {
  document  :> Document reverse comments,
  body       : Text,
  author    :> User,
  unique commentRef { document, posted_at }
}
```

`Document.comments` is then an addressable table-valued reverse relation with identical query semantics to the proposal's, and `:describe Document deep` nests identically. Everything the proposal identified as the *real* value survives — the addressable fibre, the optional `as` at queries.md:134-146, the nested rendering, the join edge.

Everything that is merely inline-declaration machinery evaporates, and that is where every one of the proposal's hard cases lived:

| Proposal must specify | (B) |
|---|---|
| Declaring/amending another table from this body | Nothing to amend — one declaration site |
| Same-commit double declaration is an error | Cannot arise |
| Origin addressing so redeclaration cannot drop the generated FK | The FK is ordinary and declared in place |
| Refusing a `:<` that adds a `:>` to a populated child | Cannot arise |
| Bodiless-vs-bodied `:<` amendment table | Cannot arise |
| `SubTableTraits` ambiguity on a bodiless `:<` | Cannot arise |
| `via` default and its rename hazard | The FK has its own name already |
| Desugarer as sole consumer; round-trip test as its justification | No desugaring — flat form IS the source form |
| At most one `:<` per child carries a body; later ones need `via` | Two FKs to one parent are two `reverse` names, side by side |

The double-reference case reads better too:

```
sender    :> User reverse sent,
recipient :> User reverse received,
```

Cost: one reserved word. `reverse` is a far less plausible field name than `has`, `owns`, `from`, or `by` — the exact ground railroad.md:938-943 refused `write` and `open` on — and it is the word every prior art in the proposal's own references uses for this concept (Django's `related_name` documents 'the reverse accessor'; Ecto and Rails call it the inverse).

**Why the split is principled rather than a compromise.** Nesting a declaration is a claim of ownership. `Component` is what encodes ownership, and tables.md:466-469 already reasons this way: 'If a row must exist atomically with another and has independent identity and lifetime, that is a modelling error — make it a component, or derive it.' So: **nest what you own — `:>` + `Component`, already legal under (A); name the reverse of what you do not — `reverse` on the child's FK.** The proposal's construct instead lets you nest a child with independent identity, independent lifetime, and its own shard placement, which reads as ownership and is not — and it then has to spend a warning ('nesting under the other end without reordering the key is a warning') papering over precisely that mismatch.

**And for the user's original grievance specifically — hiding the linking table from the call site — the answer is already written and is better than either:** the writable derived-table pattern at auth.md:476-500 and queries.md:527-557. It costs the same one extra statement the user objected to, and buys write-through, which neither `:<` nor `reverse` offers.

### Questions for you

- Should the reverse relation's name default when omitted? A bodiless `Comment` child could imply `Document.comments` (child table, snake_case, pluralized), which would let `:describe … deep` nest an unnamed inbound FK. My recommendation is no — pluralization is a natural-language guess, the capitalization convention is style rather than grammar, and Django's `<model>_set` default is the part of `related_name` people most often override. But it would make every existing FK nestable without a schema edit.
- Should the child's replication trait default to `Component` instead of to the parent's? I recommend the parent's, so cascade delete is always written; the counter-case is that most things you nest inline genuinely are owned, and `: Component` on every dependent declaration is noise.
- For a two-root linking table, should the disagreement between nesting and key order (nested under `Order`, key `{ tag, order }`) be a warning or an error? I recommend a warning, matching the cross-shard FK warning, but an error is defensible since the source text then claims an ownership the storage does not honour.
- Should a table-valued reverse path be admissible directly in an `AssertBody` (`assert hasComment { self.comments }`), or must presence keep the single join spelling (`self >< Comment`)? I recommend rejecting the path form to keep one presence spelling, but the path form is shorter and the anchoring rule already permits reverse traversal.
- Do you want `:describe … deep` to take a depth (`deep 2`), or is unbounded-with-cycle-detection enough? Unbounded is simpler and matches `verify shard … deep`; a depth argument would need a `NumLit` in the production.
- Is `Reference` child with a `:>` into shard-local `UserData` something you want ruled out now, or left as the pre-existing open case? This construct makes it easy to write by accident via `SubTableTraits`.
- Anything else you want factored in — other cases this has to cover, constraints I have not seen, or parts of the above you want argued harder?
- (from the critic) Which reading of `headers :> RequestHeader : Component { ... }` is correct — one header (tables.md:326, `:>` wraps a `DataId`) or all of that request's headers (queries.md:234-236, 'the same construct as an inline component sub-table', plus `ordinal`, document order, and the 2^32-per-parent cap)? This is not a detail of the proposal; it decides whether the proposal is closing a gap or adding a second spelling, and it needs settling in tables.md and queries.md either way. My reading is table-valued.
- (from the critic) Do you want the reverse relation declared on the parent (`comments :< Comment`, an amendment to another table) or on the child (`document :> Document reverse comments`, a local attribute of the FK)? The proposal itself concludes the NAME must be stored on the FK edge, so the child-side spelling makes declaration and storage coincide and deletes about nine rules. Is the inline-child-declaration ergonomic worth those nine rules to you?
- (from the critic) Should `count <reverse>` be usable as a filter predicate on the parent when the child carries an access assert? constraints.md:240-243 deliberately accepted visible cardinality for rows already in a result; using it in a `where` turns it into a scannable oracle over rows the requester may not read. Rule, or recorded known leak?
- (from the critic) For a `Component` child, should `deprecate <Parent>.<reverse-name>` drop the name only and never the edge? traits.md:220 says a component cannot be reparented because the parent IS the identifier, so the proposal's uniform 'retires the relation and its generated FK' cannot apply there.
- (from the critic) Should the cross-root FK of a many-to-many be reported at schema commit as coerced out of `enforce always` (open-questions.md:144)? Today that rule is stated for asserts; whether an FK functor's referential integrity is subject to it is not written down anywhere I could find, and a linking table is where it first bites.
- (from the critic) Anything else you want factored in — other cases this has to cover, constraints I have not seen, or parts of the above you want argued harder?
